1.caption: Yin Xi, the keeper of the pass, reads the book Laozi left behind. Notice that he holds the text, but the author is gone.
1.look: Begin with the open book in Yin Xi's hands, then let your eye move out to everything that is not the book: the willow, the incense smoke you cannot see, the white page around him. The printer used only black lines, and most of the paper stays empty. This is the first scene in the life of the Daodejing: a reader alone with words that point beyond themselves. The opening chapter warns that the Way which can be spoken is not the constant Way. Yin Xi seems to know this. He reads slowly, as if listening for what the words cannot hold.

1.caption: These hills, attributed to Mi Youren, are only half there; mist takes away their edges. Look for the place where ink stops and nothing begins.
1.look: The painter built these mountains from soft, wet dots laid side by side, so that no line ever closes a shape. Find one hilltop and try to say where it ends. You cannot. The trees dissolve in the same way. The painting lives in the passage between named things and the unnamed mist that holds them. Chapter 1 calls this the gate of all mysteries: the nameless and the named come out together and differ only in name. Let your eye rest in the grey spaces. They are not gaps in the picture. They are the picture's source.

2.caption: Lu Zhi paints Zhuangzi asleep on a rock while two butterflies drift above him. Which one is dreaming?
2.look: The sleeper lies flat and heavy on the rock; the butterflies are almost nothing, two flicks of the brush in the air. Heavy and light, solid and empty, waking and dreaming: the painting is built on pairs, like this chapter. Laozi says that beautiful and ugly, long and short, high and low give rise to each other. Notice how the willow strands hang down toward the sleeper while the butterflies rise. Nothing here wins. Each thing is itself only because the other is there. Stay with the empty air between the man and the insects.

2.caption: Sengai's square, triangle and circle lean on each other. Each shape is clear only because the others are next to it.
2.look: Read the shapes from left to right, then from right to left. The square is firm and closed; the triangle points; the circle opens. They overlap, so that one stroke belongs to two shapes at once. Sengai never explained the picture, and that is part of its humour. Chapter 2 says that the sage teaches without words and lets things arise without claiming them. The brush here does the same. Look at the dry, broken edges of the ink: the shapes are not perfect, and they do not try to be.

3.caption: Xia Gui puts a few trees and tiny figures on a low bank and leaves the rest as mist. Nothing here asks for attention.
3.look: Look first at the left edge, where the trees and the little figures sit. Then let your eye travel right across the wide, golden emptiness. There is no palace, no treasure, nothing to compete for. Chapter 3 advises not to praise the clever or prize rare goods, so that people are not stirred to quarrel or steal. The sage empties hearts and fills bellies. This painting feels like that kind of life: modest, settled, with plenty of room to breathe. The mist is not a lack. It is the quiet in which the small scene can rest.

3.caption: Farmhouses sit among willows on a quiet river delta in spring. “Empty the heart, fill the belly.”
3.look: Start at the cluster of thatched roofs near the top, then follow the banks down and to the right. Zha Shibiao painted this album at sixty-eight, and he made the willows with quick, wet strokes, so each tree is a round puff of blue-green ink. There is no hero in this picture and no grand peak. The water in the middle is bare paper. Nothing here is hard to get, and nothing is on show. The passage gives the sage’s way of ordering: “empty the heart, fill the belly, weaken the will, strengthen the bones.” This leaf looks like that kind of place: fed, quiet, and without much to want.

4.caption: The gu is a wine vessel whose use is its hollow. Its mouth flares wide, and its centre is mostly air.
4.look: Follow the outline from the wide mouth down to the narrow waist and out again to the base. The bronze is only a thin skin around an empty column. Three thousand years ago this cup held offerings for ancestors. Chapter 4 says the Way is empty, yet using it never fills it up; it is deep, like the ancestor of the ten thousand things. Imagine looking down into the gu from above: a dark round hole with no bottom you can see. The shape is useful because it holds back from being solid.

4.caption: A plain white bowl from the Gongxian kilns, made for drinking tea. “Dao is an empty bowl. Use it, and perhaps it does not fill.”
4.look: Look first at the inside of the bowl, which you can only half see. The potter gave it a wide, low rim and no decoration at all: only a smooth ivory glaze over a white body. The museum says bowls of this kind were used for tea and were traded as far as Samarra. Its use is in the hollow, not in the clay. The passage begins, “Dao is an empty bowl. Use it, and perhaps it does not fill.” Let your eye rest on the curve where the light falls into the bowl. That open space is what the bowl gives.

5.caption: This scroll, attributed to Xia Gui, leaves most of the paper blank. The empty space works like the bellows in this chapter: it gives, and it is never used up.
5.look: Look at how much is not painted. Cliffs and pines crowd one side, and everything else is mist and water. Yet the blank paper does not feel weak; it gives the rocks their weight and the trees their reach. Chapter 5 says heaven and earth are like a bellows: empty but not exhausted; the more it moves, the more comes out. Breathe slowly while you look. Let the empty part of the picture breathe with you. The painting does not favour any one thing. Rock, tree and fog are all simply allowed.

5.caption: A glazed clay dog from the Eastern Han, with its head up and its mouth open. “They treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.”
5.look: Start with the open mouth and the pricked ears, then follow the long neck down to the folded legs. The potter shaped it with a light, humorous hand, and the lead glaze runs over it like brown honey. Clay animals like this one were often placed in Han tombs. A straw dog, too, was a thing made for a rite: honoured during the rite, then put aside. The passage says heaven and earth “treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.” This dog is not straw, but it asks the same question. What is a made thing worth after its use is over?

6.caption: Hongren's valley is pale and still, with a thin stream running down its centre. The valley spirit does not die.
6.look: Start at the top among the angular rocks and follow the stream downward. The forms are drawn in thin, dry lines with almost no shading, so the whole valley feels open and clean. Chapter 6 speaks of the valley spirit and the mysterious female, the root of heaven and earth, which goes on and on and is never used up. A valley is a low, receiving place. Everything flows into it. Notice that the painting has no strong focus; your eye keeps sinking toward the low, quiet centre, as water does.

6.caption: Kuncan hides a monk's house deep in the folds of the mountain. Find it, and notice how much the valley protects it.
6.look: This painting is crowded where Hongren's is bare. Rock, trees and mist press in from all sides. Take your time to find the small dwelling tucked into the hollow. Once you see it, the whole mountain seems to curve around it like a cupped hand. The valley in Chapter 6 is not empty for its own sake. It gives shelter and gives birth. Kuncan was a Buddhist monk who lived in mountain temples; he knew what it is to be held by a landscape. Let your eye rest in the hollow.

7.caption: The great peak behind the temple has stood for ages. It lasts because it does not live for itself.
7.look: The composition is built on a strong central axis: the mountain at the top, the pagoda below it, the inns and travellers at the bottom. Everything is arranged in layers that rise slowly. Yet the peak does nothing. It gives shade, holds water, shelters the temple, and asks for nothing. Chapter 7 says heaven and earth endure because they do not live for themselves; the sage puts himself last and so finds himself first. Notice how the temple stands lower than the peak and the travellers lower still, and how calm this order feels.

8.caption: Ma Yuan's waves fill the whole leaf with a soft, even net. Water benefits all things and does not compete.
8.look: Look closely at a single wave: one curling line that rises, folds over, and passes its motion to the next. No wave is larger or more important than its neighbours. Then step back and see the whole Yangzi spread out flat and wide. Chapter 8 says the highest good is like water. It nourishes everything, does not contend, and settles in low places that people dislike. Ma Yuan has painted nothing but water, yet the page feels alive. Let your breathing follow the rhythm of the lines.

8.caption: Hokusai’s Yoro Falls drops straight down to the low pool, where travellers stop to rest. “It stays in the place the crowd hates, and so it is near to Dao.”
8.look: Begin at the top of the falls and let your eye drop with the water, line by line, to the foam at the bottom. Hokusai printed the fall as a column of separate blue strokes, so it looks both still and moving. At its foot, small figures in wide hats rest, and one carries a load. Everything in the picture leans toward the low pool. That is where the water goes, and where people come to drink and rest. The passage says water “stays in the place the crowd hates, and so it is near to Dao.” It does not contend; it only keeps going down.

9.caption: The Daoist Ge Hong moves his family into the mountains, leaving office behind. When the work is done, step back.
9.look: Find the tiny figures crossing the bridge at the lower left: Ge Hong with his household and an ox. Then follow the path upward into the folds of green and blue mountain, where the house waits. Wang Meng crowds the scroll with texture and colour, but the story at its heart is a quiet withdrawal. Chapter 9 warns that filling a hall with gold and jade means you cannot guard it, and that pride in wealth invites disaster. Withdraw when the work is done: that is the Way of heaven. The travellers do not look back.

9.caption: A retired official’s small house by the water faces one distant sail. “The work carried through, the body steps back: the Way of heaven.”
9.look: Start at the small house in the lower left, half hidden by bent pines. Then cross the wide, empty water to the sail, and go on to the faint mountain at the top. The museum describes the house as the retreat of an official who has left government service. The painter used very little ink; most of the scroll is mist and bare paper. Nothing here is filled to the brim. The passage ends, “The work carried through, the body steps back: the Way of heaven.” This painting shows what stepping back can look like: a small roof, some wind, and a lot of room.

10.caption: A Han bronze mirror: its polished face is gone, but its back shows the cosmos. Can you clean the dark mirror so that no stain remains?
10.look: This is the back of the mirror. The other side was once polished bronze. Start at the central knob, then circle outward past the seated deities, the chariot and the tiger, to the plain rim. Everything turns around a still centre. Chapter 10 asks a series of questions: can you embrace the One without letting go, soften your breath like an infant, polish the dark mirror until it has no flaw? The mirror was an image for the mind in early China. It reflects everything and keeps nothing.

10.caption: Two small children play beside a flowering plant, one reaching toward a butterfly. Can you soften your breath and become like a child?
10.look: Watch the children. The one on the left stands and stretches a hand toward a butterfly above the plant; the one on the right sits on the ground with a round fan and looks up at his playmate. They are absorbed and do not know they are being looked at. This leaf, attributed to Su Hanchen, catches their round bodies and quick attention exactly. Chapter 10 asks whether you can concentrate your breath until it is as soft as an infant's. The children here do not try to be soft. They simply are. Their whole being goes into one small, fluttering thing.

11.caption: A Han model chariot: thirty spokes share one hub, and the wheel turns because the hub is empty.
11.look: Look at the wheels. The spokes run inward to the hub, and the axle passes through the hole at its centre. Without that hole there would be no wheel, only a heavy disc. Chapter 11 uses three images: the empty hub of a cart, the hollow of a clay pot, the open space of a door and window. What is there gives benefit; what is not there gives use. This little bronze cart was buried with its owner. Even in the tomb, it shows how emptiness makes things move.

11.caption: A potter shaped this jar more than five thousand years ago. The clay makes the walls; the empty inside makes it useful.
11.look: Follow the black spirals around the belly of the jar. They swirl and turn, almost like water. The painted surface is lovely, but think about the inside, which you cannot see. That hidden space is why the jar was made. It held grain, or water, or seeds for the next year. Chapter 11 says we shape clay into a vessel, and it is the empty space inside that makes it work. The spirals turn around a hollow centre, just as the chapter turns around its central idea.

12.caption: Wang Ximeng's blue and green peaks are dazzling. Laozi warns that the five colours can blind the eye.
12.look: This is a small part of a huge scroll painted by a young court artist in 1113. The mineral blues and greens are brilliant even after nine hundred years. Let yourself enjoy them. Then notice the pull they have on you, the wish to see more and more. Chapter 12 says the five colours blind the eye, the five tones deafen the ear, and the chase drives the heart wild. The sage cares for the belly, not the eye. Close your eyes for a moment after looking. What stays with you?

13.caption: The poet Li Bai, who had both favour and disgrace at court, walks off alone. Liang Kai needs only a few lines.
13.look: Count the strokes. The robe is one long sweep; the head a few quick touches. Li Bai looks up as he walks, chanting a poem to himself. He served at the Tang court, was praised, then sent away. Chapter 13 says that favour and disgrace are both alarming, because both depend on others. The person who values his own body as much as the whole world can be trusted with the world. Liang Kai himself is said to have walked away from the Song painting academy. His Li Bai belongs to nobody. Notice how much blank paper surrounds him.

14.caption: Sesshū's splashed ink barely forms a picture. Look at it and you do not quite see it.
14.look: At first there are only blots and washes of grey. Slowly a rock appears, then a tree, then the roof of a small house with a flag, then mountains so pale they seem breathed onto the paper. Nothing is outlined. Chapter 14 describes the Way as what you look at and do not see, listen to and do not hear, grasp and do not catch. It is shape without shape, image without thing. Let your eyes go soft. The painting comes and goes, as the chapter says the Way does.

15.caption: In Sesshū's winter landscape a sharp line of cliff cuts down through cold air. The ancient masters were careful, as if crossing a winter stream.
15.look: Look at the left scroll first. A single dark stroke runs down the middle like a crack in ice. Beside it, a tiny temple and a figure with a hat move through the snow. Everything is still and alert. Chapter 15 says the ancient masters were hesitant, as if crossing a stream in winter; watchful, as if they feared their neighbours; simple, like uncarved wood; open, like a valley; murky, like muddy water. Then turn to the autumn scroll on the right, softer and wider. Both seasons ask for the same attention.

15.caption: Wen Zhengming painted these bare old trees over a cold stream in his eighties. “Wary, as if crossing a river in winter.”
15.look: Start at the twisted trunks near the bottom and follow the small stream as it winds between the rocks. Wen Zhengming painted the bark with dry, broken strokes, so the trees look worn but still standing. Above them is a wide field of empty paper and his small, careful inscription, which says he painted it playfully, in his eighties. The passage pictures the officers of old as “wary, as if crossing a river in winter,” and “solid, like uncarved wood.” These trees have both: the caution of great age and the plain strength of wood that no one has shaped.

16.caption: Ni Zan paints an empty pavilion between two shores. Attain the summit of emptiness; hold fast to stillness.
16.look: The picture has three parts: a near bank with thin trees and an empty hut, a wide band of blank water, and low hills far away. No person is present. Ni Zan used dry, light ink and almost no colour. Chapter 16 asks us to reach complete emptiness and keep deep stillness, and to watch the ten thousand things rise and return to their root. Let your eye rest in the empty water. It is the centre of the painting. The hut waits there, like a mind with nothing in it, ready to receive.

16.caption: A small boat comes home to a pavilion below a pine and jagged cliffs. “Each go home again to the root.”
16.look: Find the small boat near the shore at the bottom, then the pavilion it is heading for under the leaning pine. Behind them the cliffs rise in sharp, dark strokes, and behind the cliffs the mist takes everything away. The scroll carries a seal of the monk-painter Shōkei, but the museum says the seal was added later, so the painter is unknown. The passage watches the ten thousand things rise and then “each go home again to the root.” Here the journey is almost over. Look at how much of the scroll is still water and haze: the return happens in stillness.

17.caption: Fishermen work the river under huge peaks. No ruler appears; the people live their lives and say, "We did this ourselves."
17.look: Find the small boats near the bottom. Then let your eye climb the narrow, steep mountains that rise like folded curtains. The fishermen are tiny, but the painting belongs to them. Nobody commands them. Chapter 17 says the best rulers are those the people barely know exist. When the work is done, the people say it happened by itself. Xu Daoning painted this around 1049, and it has the quiet of evening. Listen for the song in the title. It is the people's song, not the court's.

17.caption: On Zhao Mengfu’s round fan, fishermen work a flat river below blue hills. “The hundred families all say: ‘We are so of ourselves.’”
17.look: Begin with the tall trees on the right, then move left across the flat, shining water where small boats drift. Zhao Mengfu filled the far hills with blue and green mineral colour, an old style that he used here on a small fan. No ruler, palace, or soldier appears. The fishermen get on with their day. The passage praises the ruler whom those below only know is there. When the work is done, “the hundred families all say: ‘We are so of ourselves.’” In this village the order is so light that you cannot see who keeps it.

18.caption: A rubbing of Confucius the great teacher. When the great Way is forgotten, benevolence and righteousness are preached.
18.look: This image was carved in stone after a design by the Tang painter Wu Daozi, then printed by pressing paper on the stone and rubbing it with ink. Look at the dignified figure, the folded hands, the long robe. Confucius taught benevolence, rightness and ritual. Chapter 18 makes a sharp point: these virtues are named and taught only when the Way has already been lost. When families quarrel, people praise filial children. The chapter is not mocking Confucius. It asks what kind of world needs such teachers. Notice the solemn weight of the portrait.

19.caption: A herdsman rides home on his buffalo through snow. Show plainness, embrace the uncarved block, have few desires.
19.look: The herdsman is bundled against the cold and hunched forward. He holds a stick out in front of him, with two pheasants hanging from its tip. The buffalo lowers its head and plods. A bare, snow-laden tree leans over them. Nothing here is clever. Chapter 19 says to cast off sageliness and cleverness, and the people will benefit a hundred times; show the plain silk, hold the uncarved block, reduce the self, lessen desire. Li Di's buffalo and rider move as one, at their own pace. Look at the soft grey of the snowy sky and the patient walk home.

20.caption: Liang Kai's immortal stumbles forward, belly out, eyes squinting. Everyone else is bright; I alone am dull.
20.look: Look at how the body is made: a few broad, wet sweeps of ink, with only tiny fine strokes for the face. The figure seems about to fall over or burst out laughing. Chapter 20 is the most personal chapter of the Daodejing. Others are busy and festive, says the speaker; I alone am drifting, like a baby that has not yet smiled. Others have more than enough; I alone seem to have lost something. Yet I value being fed by the mother. Notice how happy this foolish figure looks.

20.caption: Budai, the wandering monk with a cloth sack, grins below a long inscription. “Mine is the heart of a fool!”
20.look: Start with the round, smiling face, then follow the loose robe down to the bare feet and across to the huge sack. The Zen monk Jonan Etetsu painted Budai with soft grey washes and a few fast, dark lines. In Chan legend, Budai was a wandering monk said to carry all he owned in one bag. He looks clumsy, and he does not seem to care. The speaker of this passage stands apart from the merry crowd: “Mine is the heart of a fool! Murky, murky.” Budai’s grin shows that foolishness from the outside: no plan, no rank, no home to go to.

21.caption: This dragon, attributed to Muqi, comes and goes in the clouds. The Way is elusive and vague, and yet within it there is an image.
21.look: Give your eyes time. At first the scroll looks like dark fog. Then a head appears, a claw, a curl of body, and they fade again into the mist. The painter used soft, wet ink that leaves no hard edges. Chapter 21 says the Way is shadowy and indistinct, yet within it there is form; dark and obscure, yet within it there is essence. The dragon was an old Chinese image for what cannot be pinned down. Confucius used it for Laozi himself. Watch for the moment when the dragon disappears.

21.caption: Juran's title says it all: seeking the Dao in the autumn mountains. Find the small hut in the fold of the hills.
21.look: The hills are built from long, soft strokes like hemp fibres, rounded and calm. Near the middle there is a small hut where two figures sit and talk. That is the seeking. Everything around them is mountain, mist and pine. Chapter 21 says we can know the beginning of all things only through this hidden essence, which is very real and can be trusted. Juran does not paint the answer. He paints the long walk up and the quiet conversation. Let your eye climb slowly, as if you were going to join them.

22.caption: Wen Zhengming's ancient junipers are twisted and knotted. Bent, they stay whole.
22.look: These trees stood in a garden in Suzhou and were already old when Wen Zhengming drew them. Trace one trunk and you lose it among the others. Every branch bends, forks, turns back. Yet the trees are full of life. Chapter 22 begins: bent, then whole; crooked, then straight; hollow, then full; worn, then new. A straight tree is cut for timber. A crooked one is left to grow. Let your eye follow the knots without trying to straighten them.

23.caption: Ma Yuan's Yellow River throws up foam and spray. A whirlwind does not last all morning.
23.look: Watch the big waves rise and crash, then notice the smaller ones already settling at the edges. Ma Yuan's brush moves fast here, with heavy, curling lines. Chapter 23 says that to speak little is natural. A whirlwind does not last all morning; a downpour does not last all day. If even heaven and earth cannot keep up such force for long, how much less can people? Let the noise of the painting rise in you, and then let it fall. Look at the calmer water at the edges.

23.caption: Wind and slanting rain lash a river village in Lu Wenying’s scroll. “A sudden rain does not last the day.”
23.look: Start with the pale diagonal streaks at the upper left and follow them down across the bent trees to the roofs at the bottom. Lu Wenying, a court painter of the Hongzhi era, laid the rain over the silk in pale washes, so the whole picture leans one way. The village has gone indoors. The storm looks total, but the passage reminds us: “a whirlwind does not last the morning; a sudden rain does not last the day.” Even heaven and earth cannot keep it up. Look again at the boats tied by the shore. They are waiting, not fighting.

24.caption: The emperor's horse strains against its post, eyes rolling. One who stands on tiptoe is not steady.
24.look: Night-Shining White was the favourite horse of the Tang emperor Xuanzong. The painting, attributed to Han Gan, shows it tied to a black post, rearing, nostrils wide. All that strength goes nowhere. Chapter 24 says one who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm; one who takes long strides does not go far; one who shows off is not seen clearly. Look at the stamps and inscriptions crowding around the horse: centuries of owners added their seals. The horse is famous and still tied. Compare its tense body to the calm line of the post.

25.caption: Fan Kuan's mountain fills the sky; the travellers below are almost too small to see. Something formless existed before heaven and earth.
25.look: Stand back and let the great mountain wall press toward you. Then search the bottom edge for the travellers and their mules, tiny and patient. The waterfall on the right is a single white thread. Chapter 25 speaks of something formed in chaos before heaven and earth, silent and empty, standing alone and unchanging. We call it the Way, or Great. Humans follow earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, the Way follows what is so of itself. This painting places people inside that order, small but walking.

25.caption: In this detail of a long silk handscroll, hills and streams run on past both edges. “Great means passing on. Passing on means far. Far means turning back.”
25.look: Pick any small path or roof and follow it until it goes behind a ridge. A handscroll is unrolled a little at a time, so the land seems to have no first or last mountain. Here you see one section only. The unknown painter built the hills from many small brushstrokes and darker trees, with river and mist between them. The passage tries to name the thing born before heaven and earth, and says: “Great means passing on. Passing on means far. Far means turning back.” The scroll moves the same way: on, then far, then around again.

26.caption: The sage travels all day without leaving the baggage cart. Heaviness is the root of lightness.
26.look: Look again at this little bronze cart. It is a light escort chariot, not the heavy baggage wagon of the chapter, but it shows the same thing: its wheels can turn because the box sits firmly on the axle. Chapter 26 says heaviness is the root of lightness, and stillness is the ruler of agitation. The sage travels all day and never leaves his heavy carts behind; even with splendid views, he stays calm and apart. Notice the weight in the bronze, the low centre of gravity, the steady horse. A light, restless ruler loses his root. A grounded one can move far.

27.caption: Ma Yuan's scholar strolls along a spring path. A good walker leaves no tracks.
27.look: The walker is at the lower left, sleeves loose, brushing past willow branches. A servant follows with a qin. One bird perches on a willow twig; another takes flight. The rest of the leaf is open space with a short poem. Nothing is forced. Chapter 27 says a good traveller leaves no tracks, a good speaker makes no slips, a good counter needs no tally. The sage is always good at saving people, so no one is thrown away. Look at how lightly the figure moves into the empty right side of the painting, as if he will leave no mark there.

27.caption: Buson’s snow covers mountains, trees, and a small scholar’s retreat, and no path shows. “Good walking leaves no rut or footprint.”
27.look: Start at the small roof in the middle, then look for the path that led to it. There is none to see. Yosa Buson, famous as a poet, left the snow as bare paper and painted grey sky around it, so the white seems to glow. The museum notes warm red undertones under the grey, and birds come down into the trees. The passage opens, “Good walking leaves no rut or footprint.” Whoever lives here came and went without a mark. Let your eye travel the same way, lightly, from roof to peak and back.

28.caption: Li Tang fills the scroll with pines and valleys. Know the male, keep to the female; be a valley for the world.
28.look: The painting is dense and dark: strong peaks above, deep pines below, a stream running through the gorge. Let your eye drop down from the heights to the low places, where water collects and the wind moves in the pines. Chapter 28 says: know the white, keep to the black; know honour, keep to humility; be a valley for the world, and constant virtue will be enough. You will return to the uncarved block. Notice how the valley floor, not the peak, holds the life of this picture.

28.caption: Wen Zhengming’s deep ravine gathers cliffs, pines, and falling water into one long valley. “Be the valley of all under heaven.”
28.look: Start at the stream at the bottom of the scroll, then climb the ravine, past the waterfall and the pines, to the peaks. Wen Zhengming stacked the rocks in many layers of pale ochre and blue, so the valley is a long, narrow gap that holds everything else. His poem on the scroll answers the old song of the pine wind with a tune on the qin. The passage asks us to “be the valley of all under heaven” and to go “back again to the uncarved wood.” The low, open place collects the water, the sound, and the people.

29.caption: The ding was the symbol of rule in ancient China. Laozi calls the world a sacred vessel that cannot be grabbed.
29.look: Look at the solid legs, the raised handles, the band of masks around the belly. Ding cauldrons held offerings, and to own the great ding meant to own the kingdom. Chapter 29 warns those who want to take the world and work on it: all under heaven is a spirit vessel. Who works on it ruins it; who grips it loses it. Things sometimes lead and sometimes follow. Notice that this vessel is meant to be filled, carried with care and used in ritual, not seized.

29.caption: A Shang bronze ritual vessel for wine, cast with crested birds. “All under heaven is a spirit vessel. It cannot be worked on.”
29.look: Start at the small knob on the lid and follow the edges down to the base. Every face of this bronze is cast with crested birds against a dense ground of fine spirals, and the green crust is three thousand years of age. It was made for ritual, not for daily pouring. A vessel like this is handled with care, never hammered into a new shape. The passage says, “All under heaven is a spirit vessel. It cannot be worked on. Who works on it ruins it.” The design was set once, in the mould. Nothing on it can change now without breaking it.

30.caption: A Han stone shows chariots fighting on a bridge. Where armies camp, thorns and brambles grow.
30.look: This rubbing comes from a family shrine of the second century. Look along the long band: horses rearing, chariots crowded on the arch of the bridge, soldiers in the water below. It is energetic and full of noise. Chapter 30 advises those who help rulers with the Way not to use force. Where armies have stayed, thorns grow; after a great war, bad years follow. Gain your goal, and stop. Do not boast. Look at how the fighters are packed so tightly they can hardly move.

30.caption: A Shang jade blade in the shape of a bronze weapon, made for ceremony. “Fruit, and no forcing.”
30.look: Start at the point and slide back along the ridge to the carved mask and the small hole where it was once tied. The museum says this jade copies the shape of bronze dagger-axes, the weapon of its time, and that jade could only be worked slowly with abrasive sand. A blade made so slowly was most likely never meant to strike. The shape of a weapon became a sign of rank and rite. The passage warns against forcing the world with weapons: “Where an army has camped, thorn and bramble grow.” Here the weapon’s shape remains, and its force is gone.

31.caption: A Zhou ritual bell, silent in times of mourning. Laozi says a victory should be marked with the rites of mourning.
31.look: This bell was struck at sacrifices and court rites nearly three thousand years ago. Look at the rows of knobs, the curved rim, the dragons in low relief. In Zhou mourning, such bells were taken down and fell silent: the absence of music marked a funeral. Chapter 31 says weapons are instruments of ill omen; a gentleman uses them only when he must, and values calm. A victory is not beautiful. Those who rejoice in killing cannot win the world. After a battle, the dead should be mourned and the victory treated as a funeral. Imagine the hall after a victory with this bell left unstruck.

31.caption: A plain bronze sword from the Han dynasty, its blade dulled by age. “Weapons are tools of ill omen, not a gentleman’s tools.”
31.look: Look at the ring at the top of the hilt, then follow the blade down to its point. There is no inlay and no gold, only bronze dulled to green and brown. The museum record gives little more than a name and a date, and that silence suits it. The passage says, “Fine weapons are tools of ill omen,” and asks that even a battle won be met “with the rites of mourning.” It also says: “Win, and do not find it beautiful.” Let the long, narrow form stand alone in the dark. It asks to be understood, not admired.

32.caption: In this scroll attributed to Dong Yuan, soft hills curve around a wide river. The Way in the world is like streams flowing to rivers and the sea.
32.look: Follow the river from the far distance toward the shore, where boats gather and people wait. The hills are round and gentle, painted in long, soft strokes. Chapter 32 says the Way, constant and nameless, is like the uncarved block. If rulers could keep it, all things would come of themselves, and the sweet dew would fall without being commanded. The Way in the world is like small streams flowing into the rivers and the sea. Notice how every line in this landscape leads toward the water.

32.caption: Dong Qichang’s folded hills run down toward open water. “A likeness for Dao in all under heaven: streams and valleys, and the River and the sea.”
32.look: Start at the top left, where the hills begin, and follow their folds down to the right, past the groves, to the water at the edge. Dong Qichang set the landscape on a diagonal and built it from dry, repeated strokes, a way of painting that recalls older masters. His inscription names Huang Gongwang as his model. Look at how the hills spill into flat ground and then into water. The passage ends: “A likeness for Dao in all under heaven: streams and valleys, and the River and the sea.” Everything in this detail runs down to the low, open place.

33.caption: A small figure sits alone beside a stream under dark mountains. One who knows himself is enlightened.
33.look: Find the seated figure near the bottom. He looks out at the water, his back to the high cliffs. He is not climbing or travelling. Chapter 33 says: one who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is enlightened. One who conquers others is strong; one who conquers himself is mighty. One who knows when he has enough is rich. Stay with the man by the stream. The great mountain behind him does not distract him. What is he looking at?

33.caption: The hermit poet Hanshan stands alone in a loose robe, his hair wild. “One who knows the self is bright.”
33.look: Start with the face under the mass of black hair, then follow the pale robe down to the feet. Hanshan, the Cold Mountain poet of the Tang, is said to have lived alone among cliffs and to have written his poems on rocks and trees. Here he stands against dark branches and holds his sleeve close, as if the wind is strong. The painter is unknown. No one in the scene judges him. The passage says, “One who knows others is clever. One who knows the self is bright.” Hanshan is not trying to be seen.

34.caption: In this scroll attributed to Dong Yuan, the river winds left and right. The great Way flows everywhere.
34.look: Trace the water from the top of the scroll to the bottom. It turns this way and that, wind-blown, never in a straight line. Mountains, a house and trees all lean along its course. Chapter 34 says the great Way flows everywhere, to the left and to the right. All things depend on it, and it does not refuse them. It completes its work and claims nothing. Because it never makes itself great, it can be great. Let your eye drift with the current.

34.caption: Mei Qing’s waterfall at Huangshan bends left and right through nine pools. “The great Dao floods, oh: it can go left and right.”
34.look: Begin at the top, where the water first shows as a white ribbon, and follow it down, curve by curve, to the bottom. Mei Qing probably sketched this fall at Huangshan in 1690, at about sixty-eight. The museum says it has nine bends, each with a green pool. He left the water as bare paper and shaped it only with the rocks around it. The passage says, “The great Dao floods, oh: it can go left and right.” The water here does just that. It fills each pool and moves on, and it never calls the pools its own.

35.caption: Under a pine, a man plays the qin while two officials listen. Music and good food make travellers stop; the Way has no flavour.
35.look: The player sits with his head bowed toward the strings. The listener in green lifts his head and looks up and away; the one in red bows his head. A small incense burner stands on a stand. Chapter 35 says music and fine food make passing travellers stop, but the Way, when spoken, is bland and has no flavour. Look at it and it is not enough to see; listen and it is not enough to hear; use it and it never runs out. The qin's music was quiet and plain. Notice the stillness of the three men.

35.caption: A Song tea bowl from Fujian with a dark glaze called hare’s fur. “The Dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! It has no flavor.”
35.look: Start at the rim, where the glaze thins to brown, then look down into the dark centre. The fine streaks, called hare’s fur, come from iron in the glaze. Bowls like this were made in Fujian for whisked tea in the Song dynasty. The bowl does not call for attention; you have to come close to see the streaks at all. The passage sets music and cakes, which stop the passing guest, against the Dao: “bland! It has no flavor.” Then it adds, “Use it: not enough to end it.” The bowl waits, empty, for something plain.

36.caption: Bada Shanren's tiny minnows dart beneath a heavy rock. Fish should not leave the deep water.
36.look: The rock at the top seems about to fall. Below it, a few tiny minnows, each only a flick or two of ink, dart through open space. Bada Shanren was a member of the Ming royal family who became a monk after the dynasty fell; his fish and birds often look sideways at the world. Chapter 36 says the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. Fish should not leave the depths; the sharp tools of a state should not be shown. Notice how much empty paper surrounds the minnows. They are safe there, as fish are safe in deep water.

36.caption: Two carp turn in deep water in a Korean ink painting. “Fish must not slip out of the deep.”
36.look: Start with the upper carp, its body curved and its tail up, then drop to the second fish near the rocks. The painter used soft grey washes for the water and darker ink for scales and fins, so the fish seem to move inside the water, not on the paper. Neither fish breaks the surface. The passage moves from the soft and weak that overcome the hard and strong to this: “Fish must not slip out of the deep.” In the deep, a fish is safe and free; out of it, it is lost. The plain grey around them is their shelter.

37.caption: Tōhaku's pines appear and disappear in fog. The Way does nothing, yet nothing is left undone.
37.look: This is one screen of a pair. Stand back. The pines seem to come forward and sink back as mist moves through them. Some are painted with dark, fast strokes; others are only a breath of grey. Much of the screen is empty paper. Chapter 37 says the Way never acts, yet nothing is left undone. If rulers could hold to it, all things would transform themselves. Without desire there is stillness, and the world settles of itself. Let your eye stay in the fog between the trees.

38.caption: A Han rubbing of Confucius visiting Laozi to ask about the rites. Laozi says ritual is the thin husk of loyalty.
38.look: Look for the two figures facing each other in the centre of the band. Around them stand students and attendants, all in the formal pose of a meeting. The story was popular on Han tomb carvings: the great teacher of ritual coming to learn from the archivist of Zhou. Chapter 38 says high virtue is not conscious of itself, and so it has virtue. When the Way is lost, virtue appears; then benevolence, then righteousness, then ritual, which is the thin edge of loyalty and the beginning of disorder. The great person stays with the fruit, not the flower.

39.caption: The cong is round inside and square outside, a joining of heaven and earth. Everything that attains the One is whole.
39.look: Look at the tall, dark green tube. The outer corners are square; the hole through its centre is round. In early China, round stood for heaven and square for earth. Chapter 39 says that in ancient times, heaven attained the One and became clear, earth attained the One and became steady, valleys attained the One and became full. The ruler takes the lowly as his root. Do not wish to jingle like jade; be rough like stone. Notice that this jade is not glittering. It is plain, heavy and quiet.

40.caption: One of the earliest printed yin-yang swirls, from about 1370. Returning is the movement of the Way.
40.look: Look at the black and white halves turning around each other. Each carries a small dot of the other. Around the circle are the names of the eight trigrams. Zhao Huiqian called this the River Chart of Heaven and Earth. Chapter 40 is very short: returning is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way. The ten thousand things are born from being, and being is born from non-being. Follow the curve with your eye. It never stops; it always comes back.

40.caption: Ma Lin’s scholar lies by the water and watches clouds rise out of empty space. “Having is born from not-having.”
40.look: Find the small reclining scholar at the lower left, then follow his gaze across the empty silk to the faint peak and the clouds that form near it. Ma Lin painted this fan in reply to a couplet by Wang Wei that Emperor Lizong wrote out: walk to where the water ends, then sit and watch the clouds rise. Almost the whole fan is empty, and the clouds come out of that emptiness. The passage says, “Turning back is the movement of the Dao,” and “having is born from not-having.” The scholar has reached the end of the water and turned to watch.

41.caption: Shide, the ragged temple sweeper, looks like a fool. Chapter 41 says the bright Way seems dark and the purest white seems soiled.
41.look: Indara drew Shide with a few loose, almost careless strokes. The broom, the tattered robe and the open mouth are all you need. Hanshan and Shide were Tang dynasty eccentrics who lived at a temple, wrote poems on rocks and laughed at monks and officials alike. Chapter 41 says the bright Way seems dark, high virtue seems like a valley, the purest white seems soiled, and the great image has no shape. People who see only rags and a broom laugh. Look at the joy in this ragged figure.

41.caption: Shūgetsu’s flung ink makes a landscape out of blots and a few quick strokes. “The great image is without shape.”
41.look: Start with the darkest blot in the centre and try to decide what it is: trees, a cliff, a roof? Then look at the small dark marks on the shore below it. Shūgetsu used the haboku, or flung-ink, method, which hides a planned composition inside what looks like chance. The museum says the brush here carries the painter’s state of mind in one moment. Most of the paper is left blank. The passage lists things that seem their opposite and ends with this: “The great image is without shape.” The painting gives a landscape without fixing a single line.

42.caption: A Yuan Daoist diagram joins five numbered circles into one. Later Daoists read Chapter 42's counting of one, two and three into their own number lore.
42.look: Chen Zhixu drew this for inner alchemy, the Daoist practice of refining body and spirit. Look at the five small circles marked one to five, set in a cross, and the curved lines that join them in pairs around the five at the centre. The pairs each make five, and the fives join into one. It is not a picture of Chapter 42, but it grows from it. The chapter says the Dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, and three to the ten thousand things; they carry shade on the back and hold sun in the arms, and the surging breath makes their accord. Follow the lines back to the centre.

42.caption: The back of an Eastern Han bronze mirror: one knob at the centre, then rings of deities and beasts. “The Dao gives birth to one. One gives birth to two.”
42.look: Start at the knob in the centre, then move outward ring by ring. Around the knob, small bosses divide the field; between them sit figures that the museum calls Daoist deities, with beasts among them. Bands of pattern close the circle at the edge. The polished face, on the other side, once showed whoever held it. The back reads like a map of how many things come from one centre. The passage says, “The Dao gives birth to one. One gives birth to two. Two gives birth to three. Three gives birth to the ten thousand things.” Read the rings in that order.

43.caption: A scholar watches a waterfall pour through the rocks. The softest thing in the world rides over the hardest.
43.look: Find the white line of water falling from the cliff, then the scholar on the rock, quiet and attentive. The pine leans across the leaf. Chapter 43 says the softest thing in the world overcomes the hardest; what has no substance enters where there is no gap. From this I know the value of non-action. Few in the world reach the teaching without words. The scholar does not speak. He watches water do what it has always done: wear away stone by never stopping.

43.caption: A kitchen relief, said to be Han, of a butcher at the carcass. What has no substance enters where there is no gap.
43.look: The Commons file calls this Cook Ding, from the Zhuangzi. That is not confirmed: Han tombs often show kitchen scenes, and this may be one of many. Look anyway at the butcher bent to the hanging carcass and the robed figure who watches. In the Zhuangzi story, the cook's blade stays keen because it moves through the spaces between the joints. Passage 43 says: what has no substance enters where there is no gap. Find the gaps in the carving itself: between the two figures, under the beam. See the story "Cook Ding Carves an Ox".

43.caption: Two men on a terrace watch a thin waterfall pour through mist. “The softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.”
43.look: Start with the two men at the railing, then follow their gaze to the waterfall at the far left, a pale strip of water between dark rocks. Sōami built the scene from soft washes and a few hard, dry strokes for the rocks and the pine. The museum links the subject to Li Bai’s poem on gazing at the waterfall on Mount Lu. Water is soft, yet it has cut this whole gorge. The passage says, “The softest thing under heaven gallops over the hardest thing under heaven.” The men stand still; the water does the work.

44.caption: A fisherman floats on calm water, far from court. Which is dearer, fame or your life?
44.look: The boat is very small. Above it, a poem by the painter praises the fisherman's life. Wu Zhen was a Yuan dynasty recluse who painted fishermen again and again; for him, the fisherman meant a person who has chosen freedom over office. Chapter 44 asks: fame or the self, which is dearer? The self or possessions, which is more? Gain or loss, which harms more? One who knows what is enough is not disgraced; one who knows when to stop is not in danger. Look at the stillness of the water.

44.caption: Xu You, who refused a throne, rests by a stream under cliffs and pines. “Know enough: no disgrace. Know to stop: no danger.”
44.look: Look for the small seated figure near the bottom, then climb through the pines to the high cliffs. Dai Jin shows Xu You in a labourer’s short robe, his belly showing, one arm on a raised knee. In the old story, the sage-emperor Yao offered him the throne; he refused it and went to farm on Mount Ji. The passage asks, “Name or body: which is nearer?” Xu You chose the body and the stream. His ease shows the end of the passage: “Know enough: no disgrace. Know to stop: no danger. Then it can last long.”

45.caption: Mi Fu's cursive looks careless and spills across the page. The greatest skill seems clumsy.
45.look: Look at one character and you may not recognise it. The strokes run together, thicken, thin out, and rush on. Mi Fu was a master of every script, yet in his cursive writing he lets the brush seem almost out of control. Chapter 45 says great completion seems incomplete, yet its use is never exhausted. Great fullness seems empty. Great straightness seems bent; great skill seems clumsy; great eloquence seems to stammer. Follow one line from top to bottom without trying to read it. Feel the speed and the pauses.

45.caption: A Korean celadon bowl, its green glaze crazed with fine cracks. “Great completion seems chipped; its use does not wear out.”
45.look: Start at the rim, then let your eye wander over the web of fine lines in the glaze. Cracks like these form as glaze and clay shrink at different rates while they cool. To a careless eye they look like damage; to a potter they are part of the surface. The museum says everyday bowls like this were often placed in Goryeo tombs. The passage opens, “Great completion seems chipped; its use does not wear out.” This bowl is whole and still able to hold. Its flaws are where the light catches.

46.caption: Li Gonglin's horse stands calmly with its groom. When the world has the Way, horses fertilise the fields.
46.look: Li Gonglin drew this horse with fine, plain ink lines and almost no colour. The animal is quiet and powerful. The groom holds the reins loosely. Chapter 46 says when the world has the Way, fast horses are sent back to haul dung in the fields. When the world lacks the Way, war horses are bred on the frontier. No disaster is greater than not knowing what is enough. Look at the horse's calm eye and soft stance. It is not running anywhere. This is a horse at peace.

46.caption: Farmers and water buffalo work the fields by a summer river. “When the world has Dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields.”
46.look: Start at the willows on the right, then look along the banks for the small figures and the buffalo at work. Kano Hideyori painted with light ink and a few touches of colour, and he left the river wide and calm. The museum says scenes like this were linked with the ideal of a prosperous realm. No animal here is going to war. The passage says, “When the world has Dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields.” The animals in this scroll pull, wade, and graze. That is what enough looks like.

47.caption: A scholar sits under a pine and listens to the wind. Without going out the door, one can know the world.
47.look: The man sits at the foot of the pine, one arm resting on a root, looking calmly out to the right. Above him, the trunk twists high into the scroll. A stream runs nearby. He is not travelling or studying. He is listening. Chapter 47 says: without going out the door, know the world; without looking out the window, see the way of heaven. The further you go, the less you know. Imagine the sound the scholar hears. Let the painting go quiet in your mind until only the wind in the pines is left.

47.caption: In Chen Hongshou’s album leaf, a scholar sits in a thatched hut under a great pine. “Without going out of the door, know the world.”
47.look: Look first for the hut, half hidden under the pine, and the scholar seated inside it. Then look up at the fan of needles, drawn one cluster at a time, and out to the lake and the far shore at the top. Chen Hongshou painted in a deliberately old-fashioned, very precise way, with rocks like stacked blocks. The whole world seems to arrive at the hut while the reader stays put. The passage says, “Without going out of the door, know the world. Without peeping through the window, see heaven’s way.” He sits still; the view comes to him.

48.caption: The eighth of the Ten Oxherding Pictures is an empty circle. In pursuing the Way, one loses a little every day.
48.look: In the earlier pictures of this series, a herdsman searches for an ox, catches it, tames it, rides it home. Then, in the eighth, both the ox and the man are gone. Only the circle remains. Chapter 48 says those who study gain more every day; those who follow the Way lose more every day. Lose and lose again, until you reach non-action. Do nothing, and nothing is left undone. Look into the circle. There is nothing to find there, and nothing missing.

49.caption: A girl and her small brother play with a cat under winter blossoms. The sage treats all people as his children.
49.look: The children wear fine clothes. The girl bends toward a kitten while she trails a peacock-feather lure behind her, and her small brother reaches for the feathers. Plum and camellia bloom against the cold. Chapter 49 says the sage has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the hearts of the people as his heart. He is good to the good and also good to those who are not good. In the world he is calm and unbiased; the people turn their eyes and ears to him, and he treats them all as children. Notice how gently the girl attends to the smallest creature.

50.caption: This tiger, attributed to Muqi, crouches in the grass. One who cares well for life meets no tiger on the road.
50.look: Look first at the eyes, then at the soft, wet ink of the body. The tiger is powerful but not attacking. Chapter 50 says among those who go out into life and into death, some are companions of life, some companions of death. Those who care well for life walk without meeting rhinoceros or tiger. Their bodies offer no place for the claw or the horn. Why? Because they have no place of death. Look at the tiger. It is not looking for you.

51.caption: Guo Xi's mountains seem to stir as spring begins. The Way gives birth; virtue nourishes.
51.look: The whole scroll twists upward like steam: rocks curl, trees reach, mist lifts. Look at the fishermen and travellers in the lower corners, small signs of human life waking up with the season. Chapter 51 says the Way gives birth to all things, virtue nourishes them, matter shapes them, circumstances complete them. The Way gives birth and does not possess; it acts and does not rely; it raises and does not rule. This is called mysterious virtue. Spring does all its work and asks nothing in return.

52.caption: Shitao's traveller sits in a small boat on blank water, going home. Know the child; return to the mother.
52.look: The painting is mostly empty. The man in the boat sits quietly; reeds lean at the bottom, a few soft hills appear far above. Chapter 52 says the world has a beginning, which is its mother. Knowing the mother, you know the child; knowing the child, return to the mother, and to the end of your life you will be safe. Block the openings, close the doors, and you will not be worn out. See the small and call it clear. The boat is moving home. Let it.

53.caption: Cranes circle the palace gate in a painting from Emperor Huizong's court, a sign of good fortune. Fifteen years later his dynasty fell.
53.look: The blue is intense, the cranes elegant, the roof precise. It bears the name of an emperor who loved art and luxury and kept painters at his court. In 1127 his capital fell to invaders and he died a captive. Chapter 53 says the great Way is very level, but people love side paths. The court is very fine, the fields full of weeds, the granaries empty; people wear rich clothes and carry sharp swords, eat and drink too much, have more wealth than they need. This is called robbery. Look at the beauty, and remember the fields.

53.caption: A Warring States bronze jar, gilded and inlaid with silver swirls. “Glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus.”
53.look: Start with the small animals on the lid, then let the silver spirals pull your eye around the body. The bronze is inlaid with strands of silver and gilded in bands: a luxury for a noble house of the Warring States. It is beautiful, and it is also a sign of how much that house could take. The passage describes a court swept clean while the fields are weedy and the granaries empty. Its people wear patterned silks, “glutted with drink and food, with goods in surplus. This is called the robbers’ boast.” Look again at the gold.

54.caption: Two old pines stand together, deeply rooted. What is well planted cannot be uprooted.
54.look: Follow each trunk down to the ground. The roots grip the earth; the branches twist but hold. Behind them, a stream and soft hills. Wu Zhen painted this in 1328. Chapter 54 says what is well planted is not uprooted, what is well embraced does not slip away. Cultivate it in yourself, and virtue is real; in your family, and it is abundant; in your village, and it lasts long. Look at how the two trees lean together. They are rooted, and they are companions.

54.caption: A quiet village on low marshland, from Wen Boren’s handscroll. “Tend it in the village: its de then lasts.”
54.look: Start with the gnarled tree at the right, then move left across the low banks and the houses among the bare trees. Wen Boren painted this scroll in the autumn of 1570 with pale, dry ink. The museum notes that paths and bridges cross the land, but only two people appear in the whole scroll. It looks calm, almost too calm. The passage moves outward from the body to the household, the village, and the state: “Tend it in the village: its de then lasts.” Here nothing is torn out. The houses stay where they were set up.

55.caption: Two children bend over their game in an autumn garden, in a painting attributed to Su Hanchen. One who holds virtue fully is like a newborn child.
55.look: Look past the tall garden rock and the flowers to the children at the round stools. Their heads are close together. They do not notice anything else. Chapter 55 says one rich in virtue is like a newborn. Wasps and snakes do not bite it; wild beasts do not attack it. Its bones are soft, its muscles weak, yet its grip is firm. It cries all day and does not grow hoarse: its harmony is perfect. Notice how relaxed the children's bodies are, and how completely they attend.

55.caption: Two women play with a small child in a Qing colour woodblock print. “One who holds de within, thick and deep, is like a red child.”
55.look: Start with the child at the top centre, standing with arms out, then look at the two women whose hands reach toward him. The printer used firm black outlines and flat areas of blue, orange, and red. Prints like this were sold in the cities of Jiangnan and hung on walls. The baby is the still point; the adults move around him. The passage says that one who holds de “is like a red child,” with “bones weak, sinews soft, yet the grip is firm.” Look at how steadily the child stands on the bench.

56.caption: Zhou Dongqing's carp turn among water plants, free and at ease. One who knows does not speak.
56.look: This scroll is called The Pleasures of Fishes, after the story of Zhuangzi and Huizi on the bridge over the Hao River. Look at the big carp curving upward, its body light in the water. The plants move with the current. Chapter 56 says one who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know. Stop the openings, blunt what is sharp, untie what is divided, temper the light, join the dust. This is called the dark sameness. The fish are not explaining their joy. See the story "The Happy Fish of the Hao River".

56.caption: Unkei Eii’s Bodhidharma looks out in silence, wrapped in a few broad strokes of robe. “One who knows does not speak.”
56.look: Start with the eyes, wide and steady, then let your gaze drop to the robe, which is only a few thick strokes of ink. Bodhidharma is said to have brought Chan to China in the early 500s. In one story he met Emperor Wu, saw that the emperor did not understand, and simply left. Here his mouth is closed. The painter gives most of the paper to empty space and a short inscription. The passage begins, “One who knows does not speak. One who speaks does not know.” Notice how much this face says without a word.

57.caption: Huang Gongwang's long scroll of quiet hills shows people living by the river. I do nothing, and the people transform themselves.
57.look: The brushwork is dry and light; nothing shouts. Follow the riverbank, the pines, the small houses. Huang Gongwang worked on this scroll for several years, adding a little at a time when the mood came. Chapter 57 says the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more sharp weapons, the more trouble; the more laws, the more thieves. So the sage says: I do nothing, and the people change by themselves. I love stillness, and they become upright. Look at how the painting seems to unroll on its own.

57.caption: Farmers walk home past bare trees at the start of the farming year. “I have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves.”
57.look: Look for the small figures walking among the trees on the right, then follow the shallow stream back to the hills and the line of birds in the sky. Tao Hong painted early spring with thin washes and a few touches of green. The museum reads the scene as hope for a good harvest. No official stands over these farmers, and no notice is posted. The passage says, “I do not force, and the people change of themselves,” and “I have no business, and the people grow rich of themselves.” The order here comes with the season, not by command.

58.caption: A groom stands calmly beside his horse. Misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.
58.look: The man and the horse stand side by side, neither leading. Zhao Mengfu painted this in 1296. He was a descendant of the Song royal house who served the Mongol emperors, a choice that brought him both honour and criticism. Chapter 58 says misfortune is where good fortune rests; good fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed right. Look at the calm face of the groom. He does not know whether this horse will bring good or bad luck. See the story "The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse".

59.caption: An old plum branch, gnarled and spare, still flowers. In caring for people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality.
59.look: The branch is crooked and rough, with only a few blossoms. Chen Hongshou leaves most of the leaf empty. Old plum trees were admired in China because they bloom in the cold, on wood that looks dead. Chapter 59 says in governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. Being frugal means preparing early; it builds up virtue. This is called deep roots and firm stem, the way to long life and lasting vision. Look at the thin branch holding its flowers.

59.caption: Wen Zhengming’s old pine twists across the scroll, bent but deeply rooted. “This is called deep roots and a firm taproot.”
59.look: Start where the thick trunk enters at the left and follow it as it turns, splits, and reaches to the right. Wen Zhengming made the bark from pale washes and the needles from quick, dark strokes, so the tree feels both heavy and alive. His inscription likens the branches to a dragon’s whiskers. A pine like this grows slowly and spends little. The passage praises “the farmer’s sparing” and ends: “This is called deep roots and a firm taproot: the way of long life and lasting sight.” See how far the branches reach from one root you cannot see.

60.caption: Goldfish turn and drift among the plants. Govern a great state as you cook a small fish: gently, and not too much stirring.
60.look: Look at how each fish moves in its own direction, some up, some down, all at ease. Nothing disturbs the water. Chapter 60 begins with a famous image: govern a great state as you would cook a small fish. Stir it too much and it falls apart. When the world is governed by the Way, even the spirits lose their power to harm. Let your eye drift with the fish. The painter has not crowded them or ordered them in lines. Each finds its own place.

60.caption: A Shang bronze ding, a cooking vessel for offerings of grain and meat. “Ruling a great state is like the cooking of a small fish.”
60.look: Start at the two upright handles on the rim, then drop to the band of masks and the three firm legs. The museum says ding were made in sets of different sizes and used to offer grain and meat to the spirits of the ancestors. A small fish in a pot like this falls apart if you stir it too much. The passage says, “Ruling a great state is like the cooking of a small fish,” and then speaks of ghosts whose spirit-force does not harm people. This vessel joins both worlds: the kitchen and the rite.

61.caption: The Tang emperor receives an envoy from Tibet. A great state should be like the low place where rivers meet.
61.look: On the right, the emperor sits in a litter carried by court ladies. On the left, an official in red, the Tibetan envoy and an interpreter stand with hands folded. This meeting led to a marriage alliance. Chapter 61 says a great state is the low reach of the river, where all under heaven meets: the female of all under heaven. By stillness the female always gets the better of the male, and takes the place below. A great state gains small states by lowering itself. Notice the tension: the emperor is raised up and carried, while the envoy stands. The painting shows Tang power. The chapter asks the powerful to do the opposite, and to take the lower place.

62.caption: A jade bi disc, a treasure offered to heaven. Better than jade and fine horses is to sit still and offer the Way.
62.look: Look at the round disc with its round hole. Bi discs were laid in tombs and offered in rituals to heaven. They were among the most precious things a ruler could give. Chapter 62 says the Way is the hidden treasure of all things. When a new emperor is crowned, rather than offering a jade disc followed by a team of four horses, it is better to sit still and offer this Way. Why did the ancients value it? Because with it, those who seek will find, and those who err are forgiven.

63.caption: A plain white Ding ware bowl. Taste the tasteless; do great things while they are small.
63.look: The bowl has no painted decoration, only the soft cream of its glaze and the line of its rim. Song connoisseurs loved Ding ware for exactly this restraint. Chapter 63 says: act without acting, work without working, taste the tasteless. Handle the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. All difficult things in the world start from easy ones. The sage never tries to do great things, and so achieves greatness. Look at the simple curve of the bowl. Nothing here is hard, and nothing is missing.

64.caption: A lone figure walks under bare autumn trees. A journey of a thousand li begins beneath your feet.
64.look: Find the small walker at the bottom of the scroll. Above him, tall bare trees rise and birds lift into the air. Wen Zhengming painted this in 1554, when he was in his eighties. Chapter 64 traces three big things back to something tiny: the tree too wide to hug to a shoot, the nine-tiered terrace to baskets of earth, the long road to the ground under one foot. Look at the walker's next step. The whole journey is there.

64.caption: A traveller on a donkey and his porter set out under autumn trees. “A journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.”
64.look: Start with the rider and the porter at the left, small and just setting out. Then follow the empty, level shore toward the trees and the far water. Zha Shibiao used light, wet strokes and touches of red for the autumn leaves. The long road ahead is mostly blank paper. The passage says, “A tree that fills the arms’ embrace is born from the tip of a hair,” and “A journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.” The whole trip still lies ahead. All the rider can take is the next step.

65.caption: A dwelling hidden deep in the mountains, far from clever government. The ancients did not make people sharp but kept them simple.
65.look: Look again for the little house in the folds of rock. It is protected, unseen, not displayed. Chapter 65 says those who practised the Way in ancient times did not use it to make the people clever, but to keep them simple. People are hard to govern when they have too much cunning. Governing by cleverness harms the state; governing without it blesses the state. This is deep and far-reaching virtue; it turns things around and leads back to great harmony. Notice how far the house is from any road.

66.caption: Long swells of the sea under rising mist. Rivers and seas rule a hundred valleys because they lie lower.
66.look: The waves here are broad and slow, rolling across the bottom of the leaf. Above them, cloud rises into empty golden silk. All the water in the world ends here. Chapter 66 says rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying low. So the sage, wishing to be above the people, speaks humbly; wishing to lead them, walks behind. He is on top, and the people do not feel his weight. Let your eye sink to the bottom of the painting and rest.

66.caption: Zhao Yong’s fishermen sit low in their boats between two shores. “The River and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys.”
66.look: Start with the tall trees on the near bank, then find the small houseboats at the left, where fishermen hold short rods. Across the water, low hills fade into the distance. Zhao Yong, son of Zhao Mengfu, used the southern plan of two shores divided by a river. The water fills the middle of the painting and lies below everything else. The passage says the River and the sea rule the hundred valleys “because they are good at being below them.” The fishermen also keep low and quiet, and nobody contends with them.

67.caption: Laozi rides slowly past bamboo on his ox. I have three things to treasure: tenderness, spareness, and not daring to go ahead of the world.
67.look: Chen Hongshou gives Laozi a gentle, slightly strange face and a calm ox. He sits loosely, in no hurry, as if the road will wait. Bamboo bends behind him. Chapter 67 is one of the few places where the speaker says "I" so plainly: I have three things to treasure; I hold them and keep them safe. The first is tenderness, the second is spareness, the third is not daring to go ahead of the world. Tenderness makes courage possible. Look at the old man's relaxed hands. Nothing about him pushes forward.

67.caption: A monk holds his old robe up to the morning light and mends it. “The second is spareness.”
67.look: Look for the monk at the bottom, raising his robe toward the light to find the hole. The painter used a few pale lines for the body and one heavy black stroke for the cloth. Above him, most of the scroll is bare paper and a few branches. The museum says the scene shows the Zen ideal of practice in every moment, even the plain ones. The passage names three treasures: tenderness, spareness, and “not daring to go ahead of the world.” To mend instead of replace is spareness. Notice how calm the work looks.

68.caption: Hakuin's Bodhidharma stares out with wide eyes but does not move. The best warrior is not warlike.
68.look: This huge face is made of a few thick, wet strokes; the robe is one bold sweep. The inscription above says, roughly, "Point straight at the human heart; see your nature and become Buddha." Bodhidharma's stare is fierce, yet he sits completely still. Chapter 68 says the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, the best winner does not engage. This is the virtue of not contending. Compare the gamecock in Zhuangzi that became like wood. See the story "The Gamecock Like Wood".

69.caption: Look again at the Han battle on the bridge. Military strategists say: I would rather be the guest than the host.
69.look: This time, notice the moments of retreat in the crowd: horses turning, figures falling back toward the river. Chapter 69 quotes the strategists: I do not dare to be the host; I am the guest. I do not dare to advance an inch; I go back a foot. This is called marching ranks that are not there, baring an arm that is not there. No disaster is greater than to take the enemy lightly. When raised armies meet, the one who grieves wins. Look for the stillness hidden inside the struggle.

69.caption: A bronze dagger-axe from the Shang, its blade worn green and silver. “I do not dare to advance an inch; I go back a foot.”
69.look: Start at the point and move back along the blade to the patterned tang, where it was once bound to a wooden shaft. Blades like this were used widely in Shang warfare, swung on a long handle. Corrosion has turned the edge to patches of green and silver. It no longer cuts. The passage quotes a saying of those who use arms: “I do not dare to be the host; I am the guest. I do not dare to advance an inch; I go back a foot.” It ends: “the one who grieves wins.” Hold that line next to this blade.

70.caption: Shide in rags, with his broom, looks like nobody. The sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it.
70.look: Look again at this ragged figure. Nothing about him announces wisdom: a torn robe, a broom, a grin. Shide and his friend Hanshan lived at a Tang temple, swept floors, wrote poems on rocks, and were taken for madmen. Chapter 70 is Laozi speaking about himself: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practise, yet no one in the world can know them or practise them. Those who know me are few, and that makes me precious. So the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it. See the story "Bian He's Uncut Jade".

70.caption: Laozi on his buffalo, a boy with a gourd beside him. Those who know me are few; and so I am precious.
70.look: This is Laozi as later tradition pictured him: the white beard, the high bald head, the slow water buffalo, a young follower with a gourd on his staff. Look at how plain the journey is. No banners, no escort. In passage 70 the words speak of themselves: they are easy to know and easy to walk, and yet no one under heaven walks them. So the sage wears coarse cloth and holds jade in the bosom. The painting is reported as 18th-century Chinese; its collection is not known. See the story "Bian He's Uncut Jade".

71.caption: Huike cuts off his arm to show Bodhidharma he is sincere. To know not-knowing: the highest.
71.look: Bodhidharma sits facing the cave wall, drawn in a pale, firm outline. He does not turn. Behind him, Huike holds out his arm, his face tense. Sesshū painted this at seventy-six. The story says Huike asked to have his mind put at rest, and Bodhidharma said, "Bring me your mind." Huike said, "I have searched, and I cannot find it." Chapter 71 says: to know not-knowing is the highest; not to know knowing is a sickness. Look at the great blank face of the wall.

72.caption: A man crosses a little bridge toward his cottage, a boy with a qin behind him. Do not crowd people's dwellings; do not weary their lives.
72.look: The cottage sits among pines; the hills are soft and rounded. The walker moves slowly, hands in his sleeves, and a boy follows with a qin. The leaf is attributed to Shen Zhou, who spent most of his life in the countryside near Suzhou and refused official posts. Chapter 72 says when people do not fear authority, something terrible will come. Do not narrow where they live; do not oppress their livelihood. If you do not oppress them, they will not tire of you. The sage knows himself but does not display himself. Look at the small, safe world this man is walking into.

73.caption: A Tang dynasty star chart from Dunhuang maps the sky around the pole. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.
73.look: Look at the dots and lines: each group is a constellation, carefully named. This chart, made around 700 CE, is one of the oldest star maps in the world. The stars seem scattered and far apart, yet they turn together around the still pole, night after night. Chapter 73 says the Way of heaven does not contend yet wins well, does not speak yet answers well, is not summoned yet comes, is calm yet plans well. Heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing is lost. Look at the spaces between the stars.

74.caption: Ancient junipers, shaped by centuries of weather rather than by any carpenter. Whoever cuts in place of the master carpenter rarely escapes hurting his hand.
74.look: Follow one knotted trunk through the tangle. No human tool made these shapes; wind, frost, drought and time did. Chapter 74 says: the people do not fear death. How, then, frighten them with death? There is always the master executioner, heaven itself, who decides when things end. To kill in its place is like hewing wood in place of the master carpenter: few who try it escape cutting their own hands. Look at how these trees were left to the great carpenter, and how strange and alive its work is.

74.caption: A butcher's skilled, dangerous work. Hew in the place of the great carpenter, and seldom is the hand not hurt.
74.look: Look at how the worker braces against the weight, and at the hand close to the blade. Cutting was a trade, learned over years. Passage 74 says: to kill in the place of the one in charge of killing is called hewing in the place of the great carpenter, and seldom is the hand not hurt. The passage is about a ruler who takes death into his own hands. The image keeps it bodily: a blade in the wrong hands cuts its holder. This relief is said to be Han, and its source is not confirmed.

75.caption: Farm families give thanks after the harvest. People starve when those above eat too much in taxes.
75.look: This print comes from a set of pictures of farming and weaving made for the Kangxi emperor in 1696. Look at the families bowing in the yard, the thatched roofs, the bare trees. The grain on which the empire lived came from houses like these. Chapter 75 says the people starve because those above them eat too much in grain tax. They are hard to govern because those above them have their doings. They take death lightly because those above them seek life’s thickness. Look at the humble offering, and ask who should be giving thanks to whom.
