75.caption: Buson’s farmer shoos a crow from his grain while his buffalo wades the stream. “The people starve. Those above them eat so much in grain tax.”
75.look: Start with the farmer on the plank bridge, then the crow, then the buffalo in the water below. The museum says the farmer is scolding a crow that came to eat his grain. Buson kept it light, with tall pines and soft hills in mist. Still, the subject is a small harvest and a hungry bird. The passage puts it plainly: “The people starve. Those above them eat so much in grain tax: that is why they starve.” Here, at least, the farmer guards what he grew. See how little there is to guard.

76.caption: Old trees twist beside a cold waterfall. Living things are soft and supple; dead things are hard and dry.
76.look: Look at the trees: some branches still bend and leaf; others are stiff and broken. Far off, between the cliffs, a thin waterfall slides down without end. Two small figures stand at the bottom, listening. Chapter 76 says people are soft and weak when born, hard and stiff when dead. Plants are tender and supple when alive, dry and brittle when dead. So the hard and strong are companions of death; the soft and weak are companions of life. A rigid army is defeated; a rigid tree is cut. Compare the water to the dead wood.

76.caption: The monk Puming painted bamboo that bends in the wind and does not break. “The soft and weak are the company of life.”
76.look: Start at the rock at the bottom, then follow the thin stalks upward as they curve to the left. Puming, a monk in Suzhou, painted each leaf with one stroke, pressing and lifting the brush so that the leaf narrows to a point. The museum notes that bamboo does not break under snow or wind. It bends, and then it stands again. The passage says, “A person, alive, is soft and weak; dead, hard and strong,” and “a tree that is strong meets the axe.” The bamboo lasts because it gives way.

77.caption: A carved Han stone in three balanced bands: deities, a chariot, a hunt. The Way of heaven is like stretching a bow: lower the high, raise the low.
77.look: Read the slab from top to bottom. The upper band shows seated figures of the spirit world; the middle a chariot and attendants; the lowest a hunt, with nets, a leashed animal and running game. High and low, spirits and hunters, are held in one balanced frame. Chapter 77 says the Way of heaven is like drawing a bow: the high end is pulled down, the low end raised; what has too much is reduced, what has too little is filled. The way of people is different: they take from those who lack to give to those who have more. Look for balance in the bands.

78.caption: Ma Yuan's autumn water spreads in endless small waves. Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard.
78.look: Look at the patient rhythm of the waves, row after row, like woven cloth. No single wave is strong. Yet the whole surface moves with great power. Chapter 78 says nothing under heaven is softer or weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, because nothing can take its place. Everyone knows that the weak overcome the strong and the soft overcome the hard, yet no one can practise it. Straight words seem crooked. Let your eye ride the waves to the far edge.

78.caption: In Tsubaki Chinzan’s album leaf, a waterfall cuts down through folded cliffs. “Under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water.”
78.look: Start at the inscription at the top left, then move across to the cliffs and down the fall to the rocks in the pool. Tsubaki Chinzan made this leaf after the styles of the Chinese painter Zhai Dakun, and he copied Zhai’s inscriptions too. The cliffs are built from many dry, folded strokes; the water is only the paper left white between them. Yet it is the water that has shaped the rock. The passage says, “Under heaven nothing is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can beat it.”

79.caption: Bamboo slips from a Chu tomb, the kind of writing material on which the earliest Daodejing copies survive. The sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press for payment.
79.look: Look at the narrow strips laid side by side, each with a single column of small characters. Contracts and debts in ancient China were often written on split tallies; each side kept half. The oldest known manuscripts of Laozi, found at Guodian in 1993, were written on slips like these. Chapter 79 says after a great quarrel is settled, some resentment always remains. So the sage holds the left half of the tally but makes no demands on others. The Way of heaven has no favourites; it is always with the good. Notice the patient handwriting.

80.caption: A fisherman finds a hidden valley where people have lived in peace for centuries. Small country, few people.
80.look: Follow the stream into the scroll as the fisherman did. Blue-green hills and blossoming trees close around the water. Chapter 80 imagines a small state with few people. They have tools but do not use them, boats and carts but do not ride them, weapons but do not display them. They find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes peaceful, their customs pleasant. Neighbouring villages are so close that they can hear each other's roosters and dogs, yet people grow old and die without visiting. See the story "The Peach Blossom Spring".

80.caption: Guests come to a village farmhouse to greet the elders on New Year’s Day. “Their homes at rest, their customs a joy.”
80.look: Start with the house in the centre, then find the guests on the bridge and the boys in the yard. The museum says the boys are lighting firecrackers, servants beat a gong at the gate, and inside the hosts offer hot wine. Li Shida drew the willows bare, with a quick, scratchy line. This village is small and complete. The passage imagines such a place, where people “find their food sweet, their clothes beautiful, their homes at rest, their customs a joy,” and the sound of chickens and dogs carries from one village to the next.

80.caption: A hidden valley of farms and blossom, reached through a cave. Though there are boats and carts, there is no occasion to ride them.
80.look: Start at the old pines at the bottom, then find the cave in the cliff on the right: a small boat waits in its mouth. That is how the fisherman in Tao Yuanming's story came in, and why no one could find the way again. Above it the valley opens: fields, a cluster of roofs, trees in blossom, a lone figure by the water. Passage 80 pictures such a place: a small state, few people, homes at rest, and boats that no one needs to ride. Cai Jia hides the entrance and gives the valley most of the paper. See the story "Peach Blossom Spring".

81.caption: Zhang Lu's Laozi rides away on his ox, looking up from his book. True words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true.
81.look: The old man's head is high and bald; his eyes are lifted, perhaps to the sky, perhaps to the road ahead. The ox steps forward with lowered horns. Zhang Lu paints with quick, rough strokes, nothing polished. Chapter 81 is the last chapter: true words are not beautiful; good people do not argue; those who know are not learned. The sage does not hoard. The more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives, the more he gains. Laozi leaves, and the book stays. See the story "The Keeper of the Pass".

81.caption: Emperor Lizong wrote out ten characters from a poem by Wang Wei on this round fan. “Words to trust are not beautiful.”
81.look: Start at the top of the right column and read down, then the left: ten characters in two lines. Emperor Lizong wrote out a couplet by the Tang poet Wang Wei about walking to where the water ends and watching the clouds rise. Ma Lin painted the other half of this fan. The brush moves fast, but the characters stay plain and open, with wide space around them. The passage begins, “Words to trust are not beautiful,” and says the sage “does not pile up.” Ten characters are enough here. Notice what is left unsaid around them.

hangu-pass.title: The Keeper of the Pass
hangu-pass.text:
Laozi kept the archives of the Zhou court for many years. He watched the dynasty grow weak and its rulers quarrel, and at last he decided to leave. He set out to the west, an old man on a slow animal, and came to the Hangu Pass, the gate between the heartland and the wild country beyond.

The keeper of the pass was a man named Yin Xi. Later tradition says that Yin Xi had read the sky, seen a purple vapour drift in from the east, and known that a sage was coming. When the old traveller arrived, Yin Xi would not simply wave him through. "You are about to vanish from the world," he said. "Before you go, make the effort to write a book for me."

Laozi did not trust words. When Confucius had come to him with questions about the ancient sages, he had answered that those men and their bones had long since rotted away, and only their sayings were left. Yet he stayed at the pass, and he wrote. The book had two parts, one on the Way and one on its Power, a little more than five thousand characters in all.

Then he handed it to the keeper, went on through the gate, and travelled west. The historian Sima Qian closes the account in a few plain words: nobody knows where his life ended.

The book stayed behind. The man who wrote it did not.

dragon.title: Confucius Meets a Dragon
dragon.text:
When Confucius was still a young teacher, he travelled to the Zhou capital to ask the archivist Laozi about the rites of the ancient kings. He came with questions about ceremonies, ancestors, and the conduct of a gentleman.

Laozi did not answer the questions. "The people you keep quoting are gone," he said. "Their flesh and their bones have rotted. All that is left of them is talk. A gentleman rides in a carriage when the times suit him; when they do not, he lets the wind roll him along like a dry weed. I have heard that a clever trader keeps his best goods out of sight, so that his stall looks bare, and that a person whose virtue is whole wears the face of a simpleton. Put away that proud manner, those many wants, that eagerness and those large plans. They do your body no good. I have nothing more to say to you."

Confucius went back to his students and was silent for three days. At last they asked him what had happened.

"Birds fly, fish swim, animals run; that much I understand," he said. "For a runner you set a snare. For a swimmer you drop a line. For a flyer you shoot a corded arrow. But a dragon climbs on wind and cloud into the sky, and how it does that is beyond me. I met Laozi today. He is a dragon."

cook-ding.title: Cook Ding Carves an Ox
cook-ding.text:
A cook named Ding was taking apart an ox for Lord Wenhui. His hand pressed here, his shoulder leaned there, his foot planted, his knee pushed, and the hide and flesh parted with a whisper and a swish. Every move of the blade kept time, like the old Mulberry Forest dance, like the Jingshou movement of the ancient Xianchi music.

"Ah, marvellous!" said the lord. "So this is how far skill can go?"

Ding laid down the knife. "What I love is the Way. It is a step past skill. In my first days at this work, an ox was simply a great block of ox in front of me. Three years on, I had stopped seeing it as one whole thing. Today I meet it with my spirit and do not look with my eyes. The senses rest; the spirit goes where it will. I trust the grain that heaven put in the animal. I strike into the wide seams, steer through the hollow places, and go along with the way it is built. I never so much as graze a ligament, let alone a big bone.

"A fine cook needs a new knife every year, because he slices. A common cook needs one every month, because he chops. My knife has served nineteen years and gone through thousands of oxen, and the edge is as keen as on the day it came off the whetstone. There are gaps at the joints, and the edge of a blade is so thin it has no thickness. Put what has no thickness into what has a gap, and it moves about freely, with room to spare.

"Even so, when I reach a tangled place, I see that it is hard. I take care and hold myself in check. My gaze settles, my hand slows, the knife hardly moves, and the whole of it parts with a soft rush and sinks down, the way loose soil settles onto the ground. I stand there with the knife, look all around, and let the satisfaction fill me. Then I clean the blade and put it away."

"Splendid," said Lord Wenhui. "Listening to a cook, I have learned how to care for life."

butterfly.title: The Butterfly Dream
butterfly.text:
Zhuang Zhou once dreamed that he was a butterfly. In the dream there was nothing in him but butterfly: wings bright and lively, glad in his own easy freedom. The name Zhuang Zhou meant nothing to him.

A moment later his eyes opened. The body on the mat was Zhuang Zhou's, stiff and startled and beyond doubt.

Now he could not tell. Had Zhuang Zhou been dreaming of a butterfly? Or was a butterfly at this moment dreaming of Zhuang Zhou?

Zhuangzi adds only one more remark: surely there is some boundary between the man and the butterfly. And this crossing of the boundary, he says, is what is meant by the changing of things.

The story is very short, and it does not end with a lesson. It leaves the reader in the moment just after waking, when the edges of the self are still soft. The Daodejing says that being and non-being give birth to each other, that long and short shape each other. Here the dreamer and the dreamed do the same.

useless-tree.title: The Useless Tree
useless-tree.text:
A master carpenter named Shi was on the road to the state of Qi. At a place called Qu Yuan, “Crooked Shaft”, he passed the oak that served as the village shrine. It was big enough to shade several thousand oxen, and a rope around its trunk would have measured a hundred armspans. It rose high over the nearby hills before its first branch, and a dozen or so of those branches could each have been hollowed into a boat. People crowded around it as they crowd a market. The carpenter did not even glance at it and kept walking.

His apprentice stared, then ran after him. "Master, I have never seen such timber. Why won't you look?"

"Enough," said Shi. "It is loose, worthless wood. A boat of it would sink. A coffin of it would soon rot. Doors of it would weep sap; pillars of it would fill with grubs. No one can use it, and that is why it has grown so old."

That night the oak came to him in a dream. "What are you comparing me with? With trees of good grain? Think of the crab-apple and the pear, the tangerine and the pomelo, and every tree that bears a crop. When harvest comes, people tear the fruit from them and treat them roughly; heavy boughs crack and thin ones are dragged down. What they are good at is exactly what hurts them, and so they are cut off halfway through the span heaven gave them. For a long, long time my whole aim has been to be of no use. Only now, with death not far off, have I got there, and being of no use is what has served me best. If I had been of use, would I ever have reached this size? Besides, you are a thing and I am a thing. What gives one thing the right to sort out another? You are a stray, unused man yourself, with one foot in the grave. What can you tell about a stray, unused tree?"

When Shi woke he told the dream. "If it wanted to be useless," asked the apprentice, "why is it the shrine?"

"Quiet! Not a word," said Shi. "It is only lodging in the shrine, to keep off those who do not understand it and would abuse it."

gourd.title: Huizi's Giant Gourd
gourd.text:
Huizi, Zhuangzi's friend and favourite opponent in argument, came to him with a complaint.

"The King of Wei gave me seeds for a giant gourd. I planted them, and the gourd that grew would hold five bushels. I filled it with water, but the rind was not strong enough to hold itself up. I split it to make dippers, but the halves sprawled so wide that there was nowhere to put them. Big it certainly was, but useless, so I smashed it."

"You just do not know how to use big things," said Zhuangzi. "There was a family in Song with a salve that kept hands from cracking. For generations they used it in their work of rinsing silk floss in the river. A traveller heard of it and offered a hundred pieces of gold for the recipe. The family talked it over: rinsing silk had never brought them more than a few pieces of gold, and here were a hundred pieces in a single morning. They sold. The traveller went to the King of Wu, who was at war with Yue, and the king made him a commander. That winter Wu fought Yue on the water, and with their hands unharmed by the cold, the men of Wu won a great victory. The traveller was rewarded with land.

"The salve was the same salve. For one man it opened the way to land and title; for the family it meant more years at the riverbank with wet silk. What made the difference was only the use it was put to.

"You had a gourd that held five bushels. Why didn't you lash it to yourself as a great float and drift away over the rivers and lakes? Instead you fretted that it was too shallow to hold anything. Your mind is still choked with tangled scrub."

frog-well.title: The Frog in the Old Well
frog-well.text:
The sophist Gongsun Long boasted that he could win any argument. Prince Mou of Wei answered him with a story.

A frog lived in a broken-down well. One day he called up to a great turtle from the Eastern Sea. "Oh, I am happy! When I go out, I leap along the well's wooden rim. When I come in, I rest on the ledge where a brick has fallen away. When I plunge into the water, it bears me up under my arms and props my chin. When I kick into the mud, it swallows my feet to the ankles. I look around at the red wrigglers, the crabs and the tadpoles, and not one of them can do what I do. To be master of a whole pit of water, to perch over a whole sunken well: what joy could be greater? Why not drop in some time and see for yourself?"

The turtle tried. Before his left foot was in, his right knee was already jammed. He eased himself back out and began to tell the frog about the sea.

"A thousand li cannot give you its breadth. A thousand fathoms cannot reach its depth. In the days of Yu, nine years in ten were floods, yet the sea did not swell. In the days of Tang, seven years in eight were droughts, yet its shore did not shrink. Long times and short times do not move it; heavy rain and little rain do not raise or lower it. That is the great happiness of the Eastern Sea."

When the frog in the well heard this, he started in alarm, then shrank into himself, lost and bewildered.

hao-river.title: The Happy Fish of the Hao River
hao-river.text:
Zhuangzi and Huizi were walking together on the bridge over the Hao River.

"Look at the minnows," said Zhuangzi. "They come out and wander about at their ease. That is what fish enjoy."

"You are no fish," said Huizi. "From where do you know what fish enjoy?"

"And you are not me," said Zhuangzi. "From where do you know that I don't know what fish enjoy?"

"I am not you, so I certainly don't know what you know," said Huizi. "But you are certainly not a fish. So the case is closed: you do not know the joy of fish."

"Then look again at your own first words," said Zhuangzi. "You said, 'How can you know the joy of fish?' To put it that way, you had already granted that I knew it, and asked only how. Here is how: I knew it standing on this bridge, above the Hao."

Huizi wins the argument on logic. Zhuangzi does not try to beat him on logic. He simply points back to the bridge, the water, and the small silver fish in it. Knowing happens there, in the meeting, before anyone starts to argue about it.

hundun.title: The Death of Hundun
hundun.text:
Long ago the lord of the southern sea was named Shu, "Swift". The lord of the northern sea was named Hu, "Sudden". The lord of the middle realm was named Hundun, "the Undivided".

Now and then Swift and Sudden came together in Hundun's country, and every time he received them with great kindness. The two of them began to plan a way to pay him back.

"Every person has seven holes," they said to each other, "for looking and listening, for eating and breathing. This one has not a single hole. Let us make him some."

So each day they drilled one opening. When the seventh day came, Hundun was dead.

This is the last story in the Inner Chapters of the Zhuangzi. The two visitors mean well. They want to give their friend what they themselves have: eyes and ears and a mouth, a way to take in the world in separate pieces. But Hundun was whole because he was not divided. The Daodejing says that the five colours blind the eye and the five tones deafen the ear. It speaks of returning to the uncarved block. Hundun is that block, and kindness of the wrong kind cut it apart.

lost-pearl.title: The Yellow Emperor's Lost Pearl
lost-pearl.text:
The Yellow Emperor went wandering north of the Red Water. He climbed the hill of Kunlun and gazed toward the south. On the way back, he found that he had dropped his black pearl.

He sent Knowledge to search for it, and Knowledge came back empty-handed. He sent Li Zhu, the man whose eyes could pick out a single hair at a hundred paces, and Li Zhu came back empty-handed. He sent Chigou, the quarrelsome talker, and Chigou came back empty-handed.

Finally he sent Xiangwang, whose name means something like "Image-Gone" or "No-Likeness". Xiangwang came back with the pearl.

"How odd," said the Yellow Emperor. "So it was Xiangwang who could find it!"

The dark pearl is the Way itself: the dark, round, quiet centre of things. Cleverness does not reach it. Keen sight does not reach it. Fine speech does not reach it. The one who finds it is the one who has no fixed shape and makes no effort to grasp. In the Daodejing, the Way is looked at but not seen, listened to but not heard, grasped at but not caught. Its finder must be the same.

sai-weng.title: The Old Man at the Frontier Loses His Horse
sai-weng.text:
Near the northern frontier lived an old man who was skilled in reading the signs of things. One day, for no reason, his horse ran away into the lands of the northern tribes. His neighbours came to console him.

"How do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man.

Some months later, the horse came home, and it brought a fine horse of the northern breed with it. The neighbours came to congratulate him.

"How do you know this is not a misfortune?" said the old man.

Now the family had good horses, and the old man's son loved to ride. He fell from the new horse and broke his thigh bone. The neighbours came to console him.

"How do you know this is not a blessing?" said the old man.

A year later the northern tribes invaded across the frontier. Every able-bodied young man took up a bow and went to fight. Near the frontier, nine men out of ten died. Because the son was lame, he did not go, and father and son both survived.

The Huainanzi ends: blessing turns into disaster, and disaster into blessing. Their changes have no end, and their depths cannot be measured. The Daodejing says the same thing in fewer words: misfortune is what fortune leans on; fortune is where misfortune hides.

drumming.title: Zhuangzi Drums on a Basin
drumming.text:
Zhuangzi's wife died. Huizi came to pay his respects and found Zhuangzi squatting with his legs flung out, thumping on a pot and singing.

Huizi was shocked. "This woman lived with you for years, raised your children and aged at your side. Dry eyes at her death I could perhaps forgive. A song and a drummed-on basin go far past that."

"You are wrong," said Zhuangzi. "When she had just died, how could I alone feel nothing? But then I looked back to where she began. In the beginning she had no life. And not only no life: no shape. And not only no shape: no breath. Somewhere in that dim, formless drift, something shifted and there was breath. The breath shifted and there was a shape. The shape shifted and there was a living person. Now one more shift has carried her to death. It is like spring giving way to summer, autumn to winter: the seasons simply moving on.

"Right now she sleeps, stretched out quietly, in the great room of heaven and earth. For me to follow her with loud wailing would only prove that I had grasped nothing of how our lives are allotted. That is why I gave up weeping."

The Daodejing says that all things flourish and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness. Zhuangzi drums because he has seen the root.

turtle.title: The Turtle in the Mud
turtle.text:
Zhuangzi sat fishing on the bank of the Pu River. Two senior officers arrived, sent ahead by the King of Chu. "His Majesty," they said, "would like to burden you with his whole kingdom."

Zhuangzi kept his eyes on the line and did not turn around.

"I am told," he said, "that Chu owns a holy turtle that died three thousand years ago. The king keeps it wrapped in a cloth, inside a basket, high up in the hall of his ancestors. Tell me: if that turtle had been asked, would it have chosen to die so that its bones could be treasured? Or to stay alive, trailing its tail through the mud?"

"It would sooner stay alive," said the two officers, "trailing its tail through the mud."

"Then off you go," said Zhuangzi. "I too will keep trailing my tail through the mud."

The Daodejing asks: which is dearer, your name or your life? Which is worth more, your life or your goods? The officials offer a place in the temple. Zhuangzi chooses the river, the pole, and the mud.

three-four.title: Three in the Morning
three-four.text:
A man who kept monkeys was sharing out acorns. "Three in the morning," he announced, "and four in the evening." The monkeys flew into a rage.

"Very well," he said. "Four in the morning and three in the evening." The monkeys were overjoyed.

The acorns had not changed, and neither had their number. Only the monkeys' feelings had changed, and the keeper simply went along with them.

Zhuangzi tells this little tale in the middle of a long argument about right and wrong, this and that. People wear out their minds trying to prove that things are one, he says, and do not see that they were the same all along. That is what he calls "three in the morning". The sage, by contrast, lets right and wrong settle into harmony and rests on what he calls the potter's wheel of heaven, turning evenly. He lets both sides walk their road.

The Daodejing's sage has no fixed heart of his own; he takes the heart of the people as his heart. The monkey keeper is a small, comic version of that sage. He does not win the argument. He feeds the monkeys.

gamecock.title: The Gamecock Like Wood
gamecock.source: Zhuangzi ch.19 (Dasheng); parallel in Liezi ch.2 (Huangdi)
gamecock.text:
Ji Xingzi was raising a fighting cock for the king. After ten days the king asked whether the bird was ready.

"Not yet. It is all empty swagger and trusts its own temper."

Ten days later the king asked again.

"Not yet. It still answers every noise and jumps at every shadow."

Ten more days passed, and the king asked again.

"Not yet. It still glares and puffs itself up."

After ten more days the king asked once more.

"Nearly. Another cock can crow at it now and nothing in it stirs. From across the yard you would take it for a bird carved out of wood. Its power is whole. No strange cock will dare to take it on; they will turn tail and flee."

The Daodejing says that the best warrior is not warlike, the best fighter is not angry, and the one who best defeats an enemy does not engage him. Ji Xingzi's cock wins without fighting because it has stopped wanting to fight. What frightens the others is not its fury but its stillness.

luliang-swimmer.title: The Swimmer at Lüliang Falls
luliang-swimmer.source: Zhuangzi ch.19 (Dasheng); parallel in Liezi ch.2 (Huangdi)
luliang-swimmer.text:
Confucius was gazing at the falls of Lüliang. The water dropped thirty fathoms, and its foam ran on for forty li; no turtle, crocodile or fish could swim in it. Yet he saw a grown man go into the water. Thinking the man was in some trouble and meant to end his life, Confucius sent his students running along the bank to pull him out.

A few hundred paces downstream the man climbed out on his own, shook his loose hair, and strolled along the dike singing.

Confucius hurried after him. "I took you for a ghost, but now I see you are a man. Tell me, is there some method to treading water like that?"

"No, no method. I set out from where I was, I grew up along with what I am, and I let it all come out as it was bound to. I go down with the whirl as it sinks and come up with the boil as it rises. I keep to the way of the water and add nothing of my own. That is how I tread it."

"What do you mean, set out from where you were, grow up with what you are, come out as you were bound to?"

"I was born among the hills and was at ease in the hills: that is where I set out. I grew up by the water and became at ease in the water: that is what I am. I do it without knowing why I do it: that is what was bound to be."

Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, says the Daodejing, yet nothing is better at attacking the hard and strong. The swimmer does not fight that power. He goes with it.

wheelwright.title: Wheelwright Bian and the Duke's Book
wheelwright.text:
Duke Huan sat reading in the upper hall. In the courtyard below, the wheelwright Bian was shaping a wheel. Bian set down his mallet and chisel, climbed the steps, and asked, "May I ask whose words my lord is reading?"

"The words of the sages," said the duke.

"Are those sages living?"

"They have been dead a long time."

"Then what my lord is reading is nothing but the leftover mash of the ancients."

The duke flushed. "I am reading, and a wheel-maker presumes to comment? Explain yourself and you may live. Fail, and you die."

"I can only judge by my own trade," said Bian. "When I cut a spoke hole, if I work it slowly, the joint goes in easily but will not grip. If I work it fast, it grips but will not go in. It has to be neither too slow nor too fast. My hands find that point and my heart agrees with them. No words of mine can carry it, and yet the work has its exact rule all the same. I cannot make it clear to my own son, and my son cannot receive it from me. That is why I am seventy and still carving wheels. The ancients took what could not be handed down into the grave with them. So what my lord is reading is only their leftover mash."

The Daodejing begins: the Way that can be spoken is not the constant Way. Bian says the same from the wheelwright's bench.

woodworker-qing.title: Woodworker Qing Carves a Bell Stand
woodworker-qing.text:
Qing the woodworker carved a frame to hang bells from. When it was done, people who saw it were startled; it looked like the work of ghosts or gods. The Marquis of Lu came to see it and asked, "What art did you use to make this?"

"I am a craftsman. What art would I have? Still, there is one thing. When I am about to make a bell frame, I take care not to squander my breath and energy. I fast, to quiet my heart. After three days of fasting, I no longer dare to think of praise, prizes, rank or pay. After five days, I no longer dare to think of being admired or blamed, of being skilful or clumsy. After seven days, I suddenly forget that I have four limbs and a body at all. By then my lord's court has stopped existing for me. My skill draws into one point, and everything outside that could unsettle me melts away.

"After that I walk up into the wooded hills and study each tree as it has grown by itself. When I meet a trunk whose shape is already right, the finished frame shows itself to me inside it, and I start cutting. When no tree is right, I leave it. So heaven is joined to heaven. If my frames seem to come from spirits, that may be the reason."

The Daodejing speaks of returning to the uncarved block, pu. Qing does carve, but only after he has become uncarved himself, and only along the shape the tree already holds.

peach-blossom.title: The Peach Blossom Spring
peach-blossom.source: Tao Yuanming, Taohua yuan ji (c. 421 CE)
peach-blossom.text:
In the Taiyuan years of the Jin dynasty, a fisherman from Wuling rowed up a stream and lost track of how far he had gone. Suddenly he came upon a grove of peach trees in blossom. For several hundred paces along both banks there were no other trees. Fragrant grass grew fresh and lovely, and petals drifted down everywhere.

At the end of the grove the stream began at a hill. In the hill was a small opening, and light seemed to come through it. He left his boat and went in. At first the passage was so narrow that only one person could pass. After some dozens of steps, it opened out into bright, level land.

There were neat houses, good fields, pretty ponds, mulberry and bamboo. Paths crossed between the fields, and he could hear chickens and dogs from one farm to the next. Men and women worked in the fields. The old people and the children were all at ease and content.

The villagers were astonished to see him. They took him home and killed a chicken for dinner. Their ancestors, they said, had fled the turmoil of the Qin age with their wives, children and neighbours, and had never gone out again. They had not heard of the Han dynasty, let alone the Wei and the Jin. When he told them, they sighed.

After some days he left. They asked him not to tell anyone outside. He marked his route carefully and reported to the governor. But when men went to look, they could not find the way again. No one ever has.

bian-he.title: Bian He's Uncut Jade
bian-he.text:
A man of Chu named Bian He found an uncut stone of jade in the Chu mountains. He presented it to King Li. The king had his jade worker look at it, and the jade worker said, "It is only a stone." The king thought Bian He was trying to cheat him, and had his left foot cut off.

When King Li died and King Wu came to the throne, Bian He presented the stone again. Again the jade worker said, "It is only a stone." Again the king thought he was a cheat, and had his right foot cut off.

When King Wu died and King Wen came to the throne, Bian He took the stone in his arms and wept at the foot of the Chu mountains. He wept for three days and three nights, until his tears were gone and blood came instead. The king heard about this and sent someone to ask him why. "Many men in the world have lost their feet. Why do you weep so bitterly?"

"I do not weep for my feet," said Bian He. "I weep because a precious jade is called a stone, and an honest man is called a cheat."

The king had the jade worker cut and polish the stone, and a great treasure appeared inside it. It was named the Jade of Master He.

The Daodejing says: those who know me are few. So the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade inside it.

jiufang-gao.title: Jiufang Gao Chooses a Horse
jiufang-gao.source: Liezi ch.8 (Shuofu); a parallel in Huainanzi ch.12 calls the judge Jiufang Yin
jiufang-gao.text:
Duke Mu of Qin said to Bo Le, the famous judge of horses, "You are growing old. Is there anyone in your family I could send to find horses?"

"A good horse can be known by its form, its bones, and its muscles," said Bo Le. "But a horse that is the best under heaven seems to vanish, to leave no dust and no tracks. My sons have small talent. They can tell a good horse, but not the best. But I have a friend, a man who gathers firewood and sells vegetables, called Jiufang Gao. In horses he is not below me."

The duke sent Jiufang Gao out. Three months later he returned. "I have found one, in Shaqiu."

"What kind of horse?"

"A mare, and yellow."

The duke sent for it. It was a stallion, and black. He was displeased and called Bo Le. "Your friend cannot even tell colour or sex. What can he know about horses?"

Bo Le gave a long sigh. "Has he really come so far? Then he is ten thousand times better than me. Gao is watching the hidden springs of the animal. He holds on to the fine part and lets the rough part go; he keeps his eyes on what counts and lets the rest slip by unnoticed. The way Gao judges a horse reaches past horses altogether."

When the horse arrived, it was indeed the best horse under heaven.

The Daodejing says: the great image has no shape. The greatest skill seems clumsy.

sprouts.title: The Man of Song Pulls Up His Sprouts
sprouts.text:
There was a man of the state of Song who worried that his young grain was not growing fast enough. So one day he went into his field and pulled each sprout up a little, to help it grow.

He came home worn out and said to his family, "I am exhausted today. I have been helping the sprouts grow."

His son ran out to the field to look. All the sprouts had withered.

This story comes from Mencius, not from a Daoist book, but Daoist readers have always loved it. Mencius uses it to warn against two mistakes. Some people neglect what they are growing and do not weed it at all. Others are impatient and pull at it. The second mistake, he says, does more harm than the first.

The Daodejing warns about the same impatience. One who stands on tiptoe does not stand firm. One who takes long strides does not walk far. The world is a sacred vessel that cannot be forced: whoever acts on it ruins it, whoever grasps it loses it. A tree you can barely put your arms around grew from a tiny shoot, and it grew at its own pace.

zhuangzi-ox.title: The Sacrificial Ox
zhuangzi-ox.source: Shiji 63 (Biography of Zhuang Zhou); Zhuangzi ch.32
zhuangzi-ox.text:
King Wei of Chu heard that Zhuang Zhou was a man of great ability. He sent messengers with rich gifts to invite him to become chief minister.

Zhuang Zhou laughed and said to the messengers, "A thousand pieces of gold is a great fortune. A minister's rank is a high honour. But have you never seen the ox they offer at the suburban sacrifice? For years it eats the best fodder. Then they hang patterned silks on it and lead it into the great temple. When that day comes it would happily be some stray little pig nobody wants, but by then there is no way back.

"Go away quickly. Do not dirty me. I would rather play and enjoy myself in a muddy ditch than be held in check by a ruler of a state. I will never take office, all my life. I will live as I please."

The Daodejing warns: to fill a hall with gold and jade is to be unable to guard it. To be rich and honoured and proud is to invite disaster. When the work is done, step back: that is the Way of heaven. The ox in silk and the turtle in the box tell the same story. Zhuangzi always chose the mud.

zhang-liang-shoe.title: The Old Man's Shoe
zhang-liang-shoe.source: Shiji 55 (Hereditary House of the Marquis of Liu)
zhang-liang-shoe.text:
Zhang Liang had tried to kill the First Emperor of Qin, and he had failed. He changed his name and hid in the town of Xiapi.

One day, on a bridge there, an old man in coarse cloth walked up, let his shoe fall under the bridge on purpose, and said, "Boy, go down and fetch my shoe."

Liang was stunned. He wanted to hit him. But the man was old, so he forced his anger down, climbed down, and brought the shoe. "Put it on me," said the old man. Liang had already fetched it, so he knelt and put it on the foot that was held out. The old man laughed and walked off.

He went about one li and came back. "The boy can be taught. Meet me here in five days, at dawn."

Liang came at dawn. The old man was there already, and angry. "You make a date with an old man and arrive after him? Five days from now, come earlier." Liang came at cockcrow. Again the old man was there first. "Late again? Five more days."

This time Liang went before midnight. After a while the old man arrived, and he was pleased. "This is how it should be." He handed over a book. "Read this and you will be a teacher of kings. In thirteen years you will see me in Jibei. The yellow stone at the foot of Mount Gucheng is me." He left and was not seen again.

At daylight Liang looked at the book. It was Taigong's Art of War. He read and recited it constantly, and he became the strategist who helped to found the Han. Thirteen years later he found a yellow stone at the foot of Mount Gucheng, and he kept it as a treasure.

The Daodejing says: to keep to the soft is called strength.

goujian-gall.title: The King Who Tasted Gall
goujian-gall.source: Shiji 41 (Hereditary House of Goujian, King of Yue)
goujian-gall.text:
King Fuchai of Wu broke the army of Yue. King Goujian of Yue was left with five thousand men, shut in on Mount Kuaiji.

His adviser Fan Li said, "Send humble words and rich gifts. If Wu refuses, offer yourself." So the minister Zhong went to the Wu camp. He moved forward on his knees, struck his head on the ground, and said, "Goujian asks to be your servant, and his wife to be your maid." The Wu minister Wu Zixu warned his king against it. But Zhong secretly brought beautiful women and treasures to the Grand Steward of Wu, and Wu let Yue live.

Goujian went home. He hung a gall bladder by his seat. He looked up at it when he sat and when he lay down, and he tasted it when he ate and drank. "Have you forgotten the shame of Kuaiji?" he said to himself. He worked in the fields with his own hands, and his wife wove the cloth. He ate no meat and wore no second colour. He bowed to able men, gave to the poor, mourned the dead, and shared the labour of the common people.

Wu grew proud and marched north to contend with the great states. Yue struck from behind. After twenty-two years of planning, Yue had Fuchai shut in on Mount Gusu, and now his envoy came forward on his knees. Goujian could hardly bear to refuse. Fan Li beat the drum and sent the troops forward. Fuchai covered his face and killed himself.

The Daodejing says: a small state that puts itself below a great state takes the great state.

fan-li-leaves.title: Fan Li Leaves at the Height
fan-li-leaves.source: Shiji 41 (Hereditary House of Goujian, King of Yue)
fan-li-leaves.text:
Fan Li served King Goujian of Yue for more than twenty years. Together they destroyed the state of Wu, and Goujian became the chief of the lords. Fan Li held the title of Supreme General. At that moment he left. He took a boat out to sea and did not come back.

From the state of Qi he sent a letter to his old colleague, the minister Zhong. "When the birds are all shot, the good bow is put away. When the hare is dead, the hound is cooked. The king has a long neck and a mouth like a beak. A man can share trouble with him, but not ease. Why do you not go?"

Zhong read the letter and stayed. He only said that he was ill and stopped going to court. Someone told the king that Zhong was planning a revolt. The king sent him a sword, and Zhong killed himself.

In Qi, Fan Li took a new name and farmed by the sea with his sons. In a few years his property was worth hundreds of thousands. The people of Qi made him chancellor. He sighed. "At home, a thousand in gold. In office, the rank of chancellor. For a commoner this is the top. To hold an honoured name for long brings no good." He gave back the seal and shared out his wealth among friends and neighbours. He went quietly to the town of Tao, and there he traded and grew rich a second time, under the name Lord Zhu of Tao.

The Daodejing says: the good one bears fruit, and stops.

cao-shen.title: The Chancellor Who Changed Nothing
cao-shen.text:
Xiao He wrote the laws of the young Han empire. When he died, Cao Shen took his place as chancellor. Years before, in Qi, a teacher of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi had told Cao Shen: "The way to govern values clear stillness, and the people settle of themselves."

Cao Shen changed nothing. He kept every rule of Xiao He. He chose slow, plain-spoken men as his clerks and sent away the sharp ones who wanted a name. Day and night he drank good wine. Officials and guests came to give him advice. He poured wine for them. When they tried to speak, he poured more, and they went home drunk with the advice unsaid.

The young Emperor Hui was troubled. He told Cao Shen's son to ask his father, in private, why he did not attend to affairs. Cao Shen gave his son two hundred strokes. "Go and wait on the emperor. The affairs of the empire are not for you to talk about."

At court the emperor reproached him. Cao Shen took off his cap. "Who is the wiser ruler, Your Majesty or the founding emperor?"

"How could I dare to compare myself with him?"

"And who is the abler man, I or Xiao He?"

"You do not seem to be his equal."

"Your Majesty is right. Those two settled the empire, and the laws are clear. If Your Majesty sits with folded hands, and we keep our posts and follow the rules without losing them, is that not enough?"

"Good," said the emperor. "You may rest."

Cao Shen was chancellor for three years. The people sang that Xiao He's laws were as straight as a drawn line, and that Cao Shen kept them, and so the people had peace.

The Daodejing says: I love stillness, and the people come straight of themselves.

bian-que.title: The Physician Who Ran Away
bian-que.source: Hanfeizi ch.21 (Yu Lao); Shiji 105 tells it of a Marquis Huan of Qi
bian-que.text:
The physician Bian Que came before Lord Huan of Cai. He stood a while and said, "My lord has an illness. It lies in the pores of the skin. If it is not treated, I fear it will go deeper."

"I am not ill," said the lord. When Bian Que had gone, he said, "Doctors like to treat the healthy and take the credit."

Ten days later Bian Que came again. "The illness is in the flesh now. Untreated, it will go deeper." The lord did not answer, and he was not pleased.

Ten days later Bian Que came again. "The illness is in the stomach and the bowels. Untreated, it will go deeper." Again the lord did not answer.

Ten days later Bian Que saw the lord from a distance. He turned around and ran. The lord sent a man to ask him why.

"In the pores, hot compresses can reach an illness. In the flesh, needles can reach it. In the stomach and bowels, boiled medicines can reach it. In the marrow of the bones, it belongs to the Master of Fates, and nothing can be done. It is in the marrow now. So I no longer ask to treat him."

Five days later the lord's body began to hurt. He sent men to find Bian Que, but Bian Que had fled to Qin. The lord died.

The Hanfeizi adds that a good doctor attacks an illness while it is still at the skin, and that the sage, in the same way, attends to things early. The Hanfeizi tells it for Daodejing ch.63: plan for the hard while it is easy; work on the great while it is fine as a thread.

ivory-chopsticks.title: The Ivory Chopsticks
ivory-chopsticks.text:
Zhou, the last king of Shang, had a pair of chopsticks made of ivory. His kinsman Jizi saw them and was afraid.

Jizi reasoned like this. Ivory chopsticks will not be set beside bowls of baked clay. They will call for cups of jade and rhinoceros horn. Ivory chopsticks and jade cups will not be used for a broth of beans and bean leaves. They will call for yak, elephant, and unborn leopard. A man who eats yak, elephant, and unborn leopard will not wear a short coat of rough cloth, and he will not eat under a roof of thatch. He will want brocade in nine layers, wide halls, and high terraces.

"I fear where this ends," said Jizi. "So I am afraid of where it begins."

Five years went by. King Zhou had a garden of meat. He had the grid of hot metal for burning people. He climbed a hill of wine dregs and looked down on a pool of wine. And so he was destroyed, and Shang with him.

The Hanfeizi says that Jizi saw a pair of ivory chopsticks and knew from them the ruin of the whole realm. Then it quotes the Daodejing: to see the small is called clear sight.

ivory-leaf.title: Three Years for One Leaf
ivory-leaf.source: Hanfeizi ch.21 (Yu Lao); Liezi ch.8 (Shuofu) has the same story with a leaf of jade
ivory-leaf.text:
A man of Song carved a paper mulberry leaf out of ivory for his lord. The work took him three years.

The leaf was perfect. The stalk and the veins were thick in one place and thin in another, as they are in a living leaf. It had the fine hairs and the soft shine. When it was mixed in with real mulberry leaves, nobody could pick it out. For this feat the man was given a salary from the state of Song.

Liezi heard about it. He said, "If heaven and earth took three years to finish one leaf, there would be very few things with leaves."

The Hanfeizi tells the story to explain a line of the Daodejing. A person who does not ride on what heaven and earth supply, it says, and loads everything on one body, is doing the work of that one leaf. Grain that is sown in winter: even Hou Ji, the first farmer, could not make it thrive. A great crop in a rich year: even a slave cannot spoil it. With the strength of one person, Hou Ji is not enough. Following what is so of itself, a slave is more than enough.

The Hanfeizi caps the story with a line of Daodejing ch.64: to assist the self-so of the ten thousand things, and not dare to act.

nanrong-chu.title: The Crowd Behind Nanrong Chu
nanrong-chu.text:
Nanrong Chu was no longer young, and his mind gave him no peace. His teacher Gengsang Chu could not help him, and sent him south to Laozi. He packed his grain and walked for seven days and seven nights.

Laozi looked at him. "Have you come from Gengsang Chu?"

"Yes."

"Then why have you brought so many people with you?"

Nanrong Chu was startled and looked behind him. Nobody was there.

"You do not understand what I mean?" said Laozi.

Nanrong Chu hung his head in shame. Then he looked up and sighed. "Now I have forgotten my answer, and so I have lost my question as well." After a while he found it again. "If I do not know things, people call me a fool. If I do know things, the knowing brings grief to my own body. If I am not kind, I hurt others. If I am kind, I hurt myself. How can I get out of this?"

He stayed in the guest house for ten days and worked on himself, and then he came back, still unhappy. So Laozi gave him the rule for guarding life.

"Can you hold the One in your arms? Can you not lose it? Can you stop? Can you let go of others and look for it in yourself? Can you be a baby? A baby howls all day and its throat is not hoarse. That is harmony at its peak. It clenches its fist all day and the hand does not cramp. It stares all day and the eyes do not blink. It walks and does not know where to. It rests and does not know what for. It goes along with things and shares the same current. That is the rule for guarding life."

straw-dogs.title: The Straw Dogs After the Rite
straw-dogs.text:
Confucius was travelling west to the state of Wei. His student Yan Yuan asked the music master Jin, "What do you think of my master's journey?"

"A pity," said Master Jin. "Your master will come to a dead end."

"Why?"

"Before the straw dogs are set out for the offering, they are kept in a basket and wrapped in embroidered cloth. The priest fasts before he carries them in. After the offering, people who walk by tread on their heads and backs, and the grass cutters pick them up to light the cooking fire. That is all. If someone puts them back in the basket, wraps them in embroidery again, and lives and sleeps beneath them, he gets no good dreams. He gets nightmares. Your master has gathered up the straw dogs that the old kings set out long ago. He and his students live and sleep beneath them.

"On water, nothing is better than a boat. On land, nothing is better than a cart. A boat goes well on water, but push it on land and in a lifetime it will not move a few feet. Are the old days and today not like water and land?

"The beauty Xi Shi had a pain in her chest and frowned at her neighbours. An ugly woman of the village saw this and thought it lovely. She went home, pressed her hands to her chest, and frowned at everyone. The rich shut their gates and stayed in. The poor took their wives and children and ran. She knew that the frown was beautiful. She did not know what made it beautiful."

The Daodejing says: heaven and earth treat the ten thousand things as straw dogs.

tilting-vessel.title: The Vessel That Tips When Full
tilting-vessel.source: Xunzi ch.28 (Youzuo); retold in Huainanzi ch.12 (Daoying xun), which ends with Daodejing ch.15
tilting-vessel.text:
Confucius visited the ancestral temple of Duke Huan of Lu. He saw a vessel there that sat at a slant.

"What vessel is this?" he asked the keeper of the temple.

"It is the vessel that sits at the right of the seat," said the keeper.

"I have heard of it," said Confucius. "Empty, it leans. Half full, it stands straight. Full, it turns over." He looked at his students. "Pour water into it."

The students ladled water in. When the vessel was half full, it stood straight. When it was full, it turned over and spilled everything. When it was empty, it leaned again.

Confucius sighed. "Ah! Is there anything that is full and does not turn over?"

His student Zilu said, "May I ask: is there a way to hold fullness?"

"Sharp wits and wide knowledge: guard them with dullness. Achievements that cover the world: guard them with yielding. Courage that shakes the age: guard it with caution. Wealth that reaches the four seas: guard it with modesty. This is called the way of ladling out and making less."

The Huainanzi closes with a line of the Daodejing: whoever keeps this way does not want to be full.

lin-xiangru.title: The Minister Who Turned His Carriage
lin-xiangru.source: Shiji 81 (Biographies of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru)
lin-xiangru.text:
Lin Xiangru was a man of low birth. He faced down the King of Qin twice and saved the honour of Zhao, and the King of Zhao ranked him above the old general Lian Po.

Lian Po was furious. "I am the general of Zhao. I have taken cities and won battles in the field. Xiangru has only worked his tongue, and he sits above me. I am ashamed to be below him. When I meet him, I will humiliate him."

Xiangru heard this. After that he said he was ill on court days, so that the two would not have to dispute their places. Once, when he was out, he saw Lian Po far off, and he turned his carriage aside and hid.

His retainers were ashamed. "We left our families to serve you because we admired your high spirit. Now you hide from a man of your own rank. A common man would be ashamed of this. We ask to leave."

Xiangru stopped them. "Which is more terrible, General Lian or the King of Qin?"

"The King of Qin."

"I shouted at the King of Qin in his own court and shamed his ministers. Would I fear General Lian? But I think of this. Strong Qin does not dare to send troops against Zhao for one reason: the two of us are here. If two tigers fight, both will not come out alive. I do this because I put the danger of the state first and a private grudge after."

Lian Po heard what he had said. He bared his shoulders, tied a rod of thorn on his back, and came to Xiangru's gate to ask for punishment. The two became friends unto death.

The Daodejing says: because the sage does not contend, no one under heaven can contend with the sage.

lord-father.title: The Lord Father at Shaqiu
lord-father.source: Shiji 43 (Hereditary House of Zhao); Hanfeizi ch.21 (Yu Lao) uses him to explain Daodejing 26
lord-father.text:
King Wuling of Zhao was a strong king. He put his soldiers into the short coats of the northern riders and taught them to shoot from horseback, and he won wide lands. Then, in the twenty-seventh year of his rule, while he was still alive and well, he gave the throne to a young son. He called himself the Lord Father. He meant to be free to lead the army.

He was a restless man. Once he dressed as his own envoy and rode into Qin to take a look at its king. The king of Qin thought that this envoy did not carry himself like any man's servant, and sent riders after him. The Lord Father was already through the pass.

He had an elder son, Zhang, whom he had passed over. At court he saw his elder son, downcast, bow down to the boy king, and he pitied him. He thought of cutting the state in two. He could not decide.

On a visit to Shaqiu, Zhang rose in revolt and lost. He fled to his father's lodge, and his father let him in. The king's ministers surrounded the lodge and killed Zhang. Then they were afraid. If they lifted the siege, the Lord Father would destroy them. So they kept it. They called to the people inside: "The last one out dies." Everyone came out.

The Lord Father could not get out, and he had no food. He took sparrow nestlings from their nests and ate them. After more than three months he starved to death in the palace at Shaqiu.

The Hanfeizi says: the state is a ruler's baggage wagon, and the Lord Father left his while he lived. The Daodejing asks: how can the lord of ten thousand chariots take the body lightly before all under heaven?

zifa-thief.title: The General and the Thief
zifa-thief.text:
Zifa, a general of Chu, liked to seek out men who had a skill. A man of Chu came to see him. "I hear that you look for men of skill. I am a thief. I would like to serve as one of your soldiers, with my skill."

Zifa hurried out to meet him. His sash was not tied and his cap was not straight, and he received the man with full courtesy. His attendants objected. "A thief robs the whole world. Why treat him with respect?"

"This is not something for you to judge," said Zifa.

Not long after, Qi raised an army and attacked Chu. Zifa led the defence, and three times his troops were pushed back. The able officers of Chu used up all their plans, and the army of Qi only grew stronger.

The thief came forward. "I have a small skill. Let me use it for you."

"Go," said Zifa, and he did not ask what the man meant to do.

That night the thief took down the bed curtain of the Qi general and brought it back. Zifa sent it across with a message: "One of our men went out for firewood and found the general's curtain. We return it." The next night the thief brought the general's pillow. Zifa sent it back. The night after, he brought the general's hairpin. Zifa sent it back.

The army of Qi was badly shaken. The general said to his officers, "If we do not leave today, I fear that Chu will take my head." He turned his army around and went home.

The Huainanzi says that no skill is too slight; it depends on how a ruler uses it. Then it quotes the Daodejing: the not-good person is the good person's material.

robber-zhi-way.title: The Robber's Five Virtues
robber-zhi-way.text:
People guard against thieves who cut open trunks, feel in bags, and break into chests. They tie the cords tight and make the bolts and clasps firm. The world calls this wisdom. Then a great thief comes. He puts the chest on his back, lifts the trunk, shoulders the bag, and runs. His one fear is that the cords and clasps will not hold.

The state of Qi was once like a well-tied chest. Its villages were in sight of one another. Its temples, its districts, and its laws all followed the pattern of the sages. Then one morning Tian Chengzi killed the lord of Qi and stole the state. He stole the wise laws along with it. People called him a robber, but he lived as safely as the sage kings, and his house held Qi for generations.

A follower of the bandit Zhi once asked him, "Does a robber also have a Way?"

"Where can anyone go without a Way?" said Zhi. "To guess what is stored inside a house: that is sageliness. To go in first: that is courage. To come out last: that is duty. To know if the job can be done or not: that is wisdom. To divide the loot in equal shares: that is humaneness. Nobody in the world has become a great robber without all five."

The chapter draws its own conclusion. A man who steals a belt hook is put to death. A man who steals a state becomes a lord, and humaneness and duty are then found at his gate.

The Daodejing says: the more laws and orders are displayed, the more thieves and bandits there are.

zengzi-pig.title: Zengzi Kills the Pig
zengzi-pig.source: Hanfeizi ch.32 (Wai chu shuo, upper left)
zengzi-pig.text:
The wife of Zengzi was leaving for the market. Her small son followed her and cried.

"Go back home," she said. "When I return, I will kill a pig for you."

She came back from the market, and Zengzi was about to catch a pig and kill it. She stopped him. "I was only playing with the child."

"A child is not someone to play with in that way," said Zengzi. "A child knows nothing yet. He depends on his father and mother to learn, and he listens to what they teach. If you deceive him now, you teach him to deceive. When a mother deceives her son, the son does not trust his mother. That is no way to teach him." And he killed the pig and cooked it.

The same chapter tells a second story. Marquis Wen of Wei set a day to go hunting with his gamekeeper. The next day a fierce wind blew. His attendants told him to stay in. "No," said the marquis. "I will not break my word because the wind is strong." He drove the carriage himself, went out into the wind, and told the gamekeeper in person that the hunt was called off.

The Daodejing says: trust not enough, there: no trust, there.

king-zhuang-mound.title: No Mound for the Victory
king-zhuang-mound.text:
In 597 BCE the army of Chu met the army of Jin at Bi, and Jin was routed. The Jin soldiers fought one another for places in the boats to get back across the Yellow River.

An officer of Chu named Pan Dang came to King Zhuang. "Why does my lord not build a war monument? Gather the Jin dead and raise a great mound over them. I have heard that one who defeats an enemy must show it to his sons and grandsons, so that they do not forget the deeds of war."

"This is not something that you understand," said the king. "Look at the written character for war. It is made of 'stop' and 'spear'." The Zuozhuan gives his words as 止戈為武. "War is for seven things: to forbid violence, to put away weapons, to keep what is great, to settle the work, to give the people rest, to bring the many into accord, and to make wealth grow. I have caused the bones of the men of two states to lie in the open. That is violence. I have shown my weapons to frighten the lords. That is not putting weapons away. Of the seven, I have not one. What would I show to my sons and grandsons?

"In old times the wise kings struck down the disrespectful. They took the worst of them and buried them under a mound as a great punishment. Here there is no criminal. These people all gave their loyalty and died for their lord's command. How can I make a mound of them?"

He made an offering to the River. He built a shrine to his forefathers and reported there that the task was done. Then he went home.

The Daodejing says: a battle won: observe it with the rites of mourning.

lin-hui-jade.title: Lin Hui Drops the Jade
lin-hui-jade.text:
Confucius said to Zisang Hu, "I was driven out of Lu twice. In Song they cut down the tree where I sat. In Wei they wiped out my footprints. I was in want in Shang and Zhou, and surrounded between Chen and Cai. And through all these troubles my kin have grown more distant and my friends and followers have drifted away. Why is that?"

"Have you not heard about the man of Jia who fled?" said Zisang Hu. "His name was Lin Hui. He threw away a disc of jade worth a thousand in gold, put his baby on his back, and ran. Someone asked him, 'Did you think of the price? A baby is worth little. Did you think of the burden? A baby is a great burden. Why throw away the jade and carry the baby?' Lin Hui said, 'The jade and I were joined by profit. This child and I are joined by heaven.'

"Things that profit joins throw one another away when trouble presses. Things that heaven joins hold on to one another when trouble presses. The friendship of a noble person is bland, like water. The friendship of a small person is sweet, like new wine. The bland one grows close. The sweet one breaks off."

"I accept the teaching with respect," said Confucius. He walked home slowly and at ease. He gave up his studies and put away his books. His students no longer bowed before him, and their love for him grew.

The Daodejing says: the Dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! It has no flavor.

xu-you.title: Xu You Refuses the World
xu-you.text:
The sage king Yao wanted to hand all under heaven to the hermit Xu You.

"The sun and moon are up," said Yao, "and the torch is still burning. Is it not hard for the torch to give light? The rain falls in its season, and a man is still carrying water to the fields. Is that not wasted work? If you took the throne, the world would be in order. Yet I still sit in the seat. I look at myself and see what I lack. Please take the world."

"You govern the world," said Xu You, "and the world is already governed. If I took your place now, would I do it for the name? The name is the guest of the real thing. Shall I be a guest?

"The wren nests in the deep forest and uses no more than one branch. The mole drinks at the river and takes no more than a bellyful. Go home, my lord, and rest. I have no use for the world.

"The cook may not be keeping his kitchen in order. Even so, the priest and the stand-in for the dead do not step over the wine jars and the meat stands to do his work for him."

The Daodejing says: once the names are there, it is time to know where to stop.

chen-sheng.title: Late Is Death, Revolt Is Death
chen-sheng.text:
In the seventh month of 209 BCE, nine hundred poor men were called up to guard the frontier at Yuyang. On the march they camped at Daze village. Heavy rain fell, the road was cut, and they saw that they could not reach the post by the set day. Under the law of Qin, all who came late were to lose their heads.

Two of the squad leaders, Chen Sheng and Wu Guang, talked it over. "If we run, we die. If we start a great undertaking, we die. Death either way. Why not die for a state of our own?"

They prepared the men. They wrote "Chen Sheng will be king" in red on a piece of silk and put it in the belly of a fish that the soldiers bought for dinner. At night Wu Guang hid by a shrine near the camp, lit a fire, and called out like a fox: "Great Chu will rise. Chen Sheng will be king." In the morning the soldiers pointed at Chen Sheng and whispered.

Then Wu Guang provoked one of the officers, who was drunk, into flogging him. The officer drew his sword. Wu Guang took it and killed him. Chen Sheng helped, and they killed both officers.

They called the men together. "You have all met with this rain, and you are all late. The late lose their heads. And even if you are spared, six or seven of every ten frontier guards die. If a brave man dies, let it be for a great name. Are kings and lords, generals and ministers, a breed apart?" The Shiji gives this last line as 王侯將相寧有種乎.

"We accept your command," said the men. Within three years Qin had fallen.

The Daodejing says: the people do not fear death. How, then, frighten them with death?

feng-xuan.title: Feng Xuan Burns the Tallies
feng-xuan.source: Zhanguo ce, Stratagems of Qi 4; Shiji 75 tells it differently, calls him Feng Huan, and has him burn only the tallies of those too poor to pay
feng-xuan.text:
Lord Mengchang of Qi kept many guests in his house. The people of his fief, Xue, owed him money. He asked which of his guests could keep accounts and collect the debts. A poor guest named Feng Xuan signed his name.

Feng Xuan asked, "When the debts are all in, what shall I buy with the money?"

"Look at what my house has little of," said the lord.

Feng Xuan drove to Xue. He had the officials call in everyone who owed money, and each debtor brought his half of the tally to be matched. When all the tallies were matched, Feng Xuan stood up. He declared, as if by the lord's order, that the debts were a gift to the people. Then he burned the tallies. The people shouted, "Ten thousand years!"

He drove straight back. The lord was surprised at his speed. "Are the debts collected? What did you buy?"

"You told me to look at what your house has little of. Your palace is piled with treasure, and your stables are full. What your house has little of is right dealing. So I bought right dealing for you."

"How does one buy that?"

"You have only this small Xue, and you do not care for its people as your children. You treat them as a merchant treats a market. I gave them the debts and burned the tallies."

The lord was not pleased. "Enough, sir."

A year later the King of Qi dismissed him, and he went to Xue. He was still a hundred li away when the people came out to meet him on the road, the old on their arms and the children by the hand. He turned to Feng Xuan. "Today I see what you bought for me."

The Daodejing says: the sage holds the left tally and makes no claim on anyone.

jie-zhitui.title: Jie Zhitui Asks for Nothing
jie-zhitui.text:
Chong'er, a prince of Jin, lived in exile for nineteen years. A few men followed him through all of it. When he came home and ruled as Duke Wen, he rewarded those who had gone with him. Jie Zhitui had gone with him. He said nothing about a reward, and no reward came to him.

Jie Zhitui said to his mother, "Of the old duke's sons, only our lord is left. Heaven has not ended the line of Jin, so there had to be a ruler. Who else could it be? Heaven set him up. Yet these gentlemen think it was their own strength. To steal a person's goods is called robbery. What is it, then, to take the work of heaven and call it one's own? I find it hard to live among them."

"Why not ask as well?" said his mother. "If you die like this, whom will you blame?"

"To copy a fault that I have condemned would be worse. And I have spoken with resentment. I will not eat his food."

"Then at least let him know. What of that?"

"Words are the ornament of the body. My body is about to go into hiding. Why ornament it? That would be to seek notice."

"Can you really be like this?" said his mother. "Then I will go into hiding with you."

They went away and lived hidden until they died. The duke looked for him and could not find him. He set aside the fields of Mianshang in his name. "Let this record my fault," he said, "and honour a good man."

Later tellings add a forest fire that the duke lit to drive him out. The Zuozhuan does not have it.

The Daodejing says: the work is complete; it does not name it "mine".

well-sweep.title: The Gardener and the Well-Sweep
well-sweep.text:
Zigong, a student of Confucius, was travelling through the country south of the Han River. He saw an old man at work in a vegetable garden. The old man had dug a sloping tunnel down to his well. He went in, came out with a jar of water in his arms, and poured it on the beds. He puffed and strained, and for all his labour very little was done.

"There is a machine for this," said Zigong. "In one day it waters a hundred beds. It takes little strength and does a great deal. Would you not like one, sir?"

The gardener looked up. "How does it work?"

"It is a wooden arm, heavy at the back and light at the front. It lifts the water as if it were pulling it out, so fast that it seems to boil over. It is called a well-sweep."

The gardener's face flushed with anger. Then he laughed. "I heard this from my teacher. Where there are machines, there will be machine business. Where there is machine business, there will be a machine heart. With a machine heart in the chest, what is pure and plain is no longer whole. Then the spirit does not settle, and what has an unsettled spirit, the Dao does not carry. It is not that I do not know of your machine. I would be ashamed to use it."

Zigong was abashed. He looked down and gave no answer. He walked on, pale and not himself, and he had gone thirty li before he recovered.

The Daodejing says: the more craft and skill people have, the more strange things arise.

zhaozhou-tea.title: Wash Your Bowl, Have Some Tea
zhaozhou-tea.source: Wumenguan (The Gateless Barrier), case 7; the tea story is in the Chan records of Zhaozhou Congshen (Wudeng huiyuan)
zhaozhou-tea.text:
In Tang times the Chan master Congshen lived at a temple in Zhaozhou, and people called him by the name of the place.

A monk came to him and said, "I have only just entered the monastery. I beg the master to teach me."

"Have you eaten your rice gruel?" said Zhaozhou.

"I have eaten."

"Then go and wash your bowl."

The record says that the monk understood something.

Another time, Zhaozhou asked a monk who had just arrived, "Have you been here before?"

"I have been here."

"Go and have some tea."

He asked the second the same question.

"I have not been here."

"Go and have some tea."

Later the prior of the temple came to him. "To the one who had been here, you said, 'Go and have some tea.' To the one who had not been here, you also said, 'Go and have some tea.' Why?"

"Prior!" called Zhaozhou.

"Yes?" said the prior.

"Go and have some tea."

Zhaozhou gives no explanation. The Daodejing says: the Dao, as it comes out of the mouth: bland! It has no flavor.

king-tai-leaves-bin.title: King Tai Leaves Bin
king-tai-leaves-bin.source: Mencius 1B:15; also told in Zhuangzi ch.28 (Rangwang)
king-tai-leaves-bin.text:
Long before the house of Zhou ruled, its ancestor King Tai lived with his people in the land of Bin. The Di tribes raided them.

King Tai gave the Di furs and silk. The raids did not stop. He gave them dogs and horses. The raids did not stop. He gave them pearls and jade. The raids did not stop.

He called the elders together. "What the Di want is our land. I have heard that a ruler does not harm people with the thing that is meant to feed them. Why should you worry about having no lord? I am going to leave."

In the Zhuangzi he says more. "To live beside a man's older brother and have the younger brother killed, to live beside a father and have his son killed: I cannot bear it. Stay here, all of you, and do your best. What difference is there between being my subjects and being subjects of the Di?"

He took his staff and left Bin. He crossed Mount Liang and settled at the foot of Mount Qi.

The people of Bin said, "This is a humane man. We must not lose him." Mencius says that they followed him like a crowd on its way to market. In the Zhuangzi they go after him in an unbroken line. A new state grew up under Mount Qi, and from it, generations later, came the kings of Zhou.

The Daodejing says: all under heaven are glad to push the sage forward and do not tire.
